4. Rumour scatters itself through the troubled cities of Ausonia,
that the cloud-bearing mountains and the crags that threaten heaven
have taken the yoke, that the Carthaginians have been carried over trackless ways,
and that their leader, boasting deeds to rival the labour of Hercules,
has come down upon them. Wicked Rumour sings of dreadful upheavals,
and swells as she goes, swifter than the winged East Wind,
and shakes the stunned strongholds with terrifying reports.
Docile fear feeds the people's rumour upon what it hears,
piling emptiness on emptiness: men rush into the bitter
cares of war in haste, and suddenly throughout all
Ausonia Mars roars and rouses arms and men.
They forge new javelins, and the steel's fierce gleam,
its rust scoured off, is donned again; they restore
to laid-by helmets the snow-white glory of the crest; the spear is fitted
with its thong, and from a fresh forge the axes are called back.
The breastplate is woven, impenetrable guard of the flanks,
fated to bear many a blow and many a wound made vain.
Some watch over the bow, some break with the lash
the panting horse into its circles, and whet the sword on the stone.
Nor do they delay to bring help to the walls
with which old age has wrestled; they haul up stones and pull back
the hollow towers that length of years has eaten away.
From these the strongholds take their weapons, and they strive to bring
oak for the gates and trusty bars from the forest,
and they ring them with ditches. The taskmaster Fear, no sluggard,
hurries all things on, and the broad fields are loud with alarm.
They have abandoned the hearth: stunned, they carry on their shoulders
their ailing mothers, and the aged old men, who draw out
their last thread of life, are snatched away; then with hair unbound
the wife is driven before them, and to right and left are dragged
the little children, keeping no even order as they go.
So the crowd; and fear is passed from hand to hand, no source is asked.
But the senators, though the monstrous undertaking terrifies them,
and war in their very bosom, and the Alps and their passable rocks
have failed them, still raise against these hardships a stern,
unbroken mind, and lift up their great spirits. It is their joy
to go through dangers to glory and to found by the right hand
a name worth remembering, such as Fortune never gave
to men in her favouring moods.

But the leader of Libya cherishes his troops behind a safe rampart,
weary of march and numb in their sinews from much frost,
and, by way of comfort, points out to them, glad,
that a road still remains across the plains to the city, and Rome within his reach.
Yet he does not think it good to let the cares of state
and the counsels of war stand idle, nor can he alone endure repose.
In ancient times, among the old ages, warlike nations
once invaded the side of Ausonia and won
themselves blessed seats and made themselves feared by the hand of arms. Then impious wars
the Tarpeian father and the captured Quirites felt.
While he stirs them with gifts, and warms their empty hearts
and their nation loose in its ways, and joins their arms to his,
already the consul, sailing past the shores in a swift fleet,
Scipio was bringing himself back from the Phocaean coast,
and the mighty leaders, having measured out the toil
of sea and of land in opposite ways, were now drawing nearer
to dangers closer to the rampart, and the first beginnings of a great disaster were at hand.
For when, the camps drawn together as the consul advanced,
Fortune had taken away delay, and the cohorts, kindled
at the sight of the foe, demanded the signal for their fury,
the Tyrian leader, in a great voice, sounds through his numerous columns
that all is conquered far and wide, whatever bears the name of Iberian:
that neither the Pyrenees nor the fierce Rhone
spurned his orders, that Rutulian Saguntum smoked in ashes,
that his march was forced through the Celts, and that where it had been a labour
for the son of Amphitryon to set his step, there under arms
the Carthaginian squadrons had gone, and the horseman, borne over the heights,
had trampled the ridge, and the Alps had echoed with neighing.

Against him the consul calls his own men to noble trial:
"You have, soldier, a foe broken and scorched by the snowy
crags, dragging along with difficulty his numbed limbs.
Come now, let him who leaped across the sacred mountains and the deep cliffs
learn how much more loftily our rampart stands
than the Herculean height, and whether it is more to scale the hills
or to break your ranks. Let him grant rumour its empty boast,
so long as, when the battle is poured out and he rushes back
the way he came, the Alps stand in his path. Over the heights
the gods have driven him on and led him here, that he might dye
the bounds of Latium with his blood, and that a hostile land might hide his bones.
I would gladly learn whether now a new and second Carthage
sends out this war against us, or the same that lies sunk
beneath the sea, buried in the vast deep among the Aegates."
This he says, and turns his column toward the waves of Ticinus.
Clear Ticinus keeps its waters sky-blue and its pools,
with their shallow bed, never knowing to be stirred,
and slowly draws its bright liquid in a green stream.
You would scarcely believe it glides: so gentle between its shady banks,
amid the tuneful rivalry of the birds' song,
it leads its sleep-bringing water in a shining flood.

And now, as the shadows fled at the very edge of night,
the light was at hand, and Sleep had finished out his hours.
The consul was preparing to explore the ground, the nature
of the neighbouring hill, and what kind of soil the plains might have.
Equal zeal was in the Carthaginian, and like cares in his breast.
And so they were at hand, with swift wings of cavalry attending them.
But when the clouds of stirred-up dust had shown
that the foe was advancing, and nearer and nearer the ground
groaned with the ringing horn of hooves, and at the same time the keen
neighing of the conquering horses raged louder than the trumpets,
"To arms, men, seize your arms, men! Both leaders press on!"
In both was swift valour and a twin desire
for praise, and a madness for battle and war alike resolved.
No delay. Now only so much field divided them from striking range
as a hurled lance, driven by its thong, can reach,
when suddenly, from a clear sky with no clouds at all,
an omen turned their minds and eyes toward the stars.
A hawk, holding its way from the mid-path of the sun,
was violently troubling the birds beloved of Venus
and famed for the honour of Dione, and with talons,
now with beak, now with hard buffets of the wing,
it had given fifteen of them to death amid its cruel wounds.
Nor was there end or surfeit, but a thirst for new blood
kept swelling, and now it pressed the dove, trembling at the slaughter
of those before, and uncertain in her flight as the feathers slipped,
until the bird of Jove, coming from the eastern source of Phoebus,
forced it at last to turn its back into the thin clouds.
Then victorious it turned its glad flight toward the Roman standards,
and where the fair son of the leader, young Scipio,
was brandishing arms with his boyish arms,
it gave its cry twice and three times, and grazing with its beak
the gleaming crest of his helmet, returned itself to the stars.

Liger cried out (his was the art of feeling the gods' warnings
and of showing things to come, the bird his teacher):
"Carthaginian, for twice eight years within Italy's bounds,
like the bold bird, you will hunt the youth
of Ausonia, and carry off much plunder with blood.
But check your threats: the armour-bearer of Jove, see,
denies you the realm of Daunus. I know you, highest of the gods:
be at hand, father, and confirm the omen of your bird.
For for you, unless the soaring bird with empty flight
falsely belies the gods, are kept, my boy, the last
fates of subdued Libya and a name greater than Carthage."
Against him Bogus sings glad omens to the Tyrian king,
that the favouring hawk and the birds slain in the cloud
portend disaster to the sons of Aeneas and to the race of Venus.
Then he is first to hurl, as if a god urged him on
and he were privy to the fates, his spear at the foe as its companion.
That spear, flying far through the open spaces of the broad field,
would have lost its blow for the distance, had not Catus,
his reins loosed, while he strives to pluck the glory of the first fight,
borne his headlong horse's face into its path.
So, growing faint and now about to fall, the cornel shaft
found the wound it sought and took its slaughter from the foe,
and stood between the temples of the brow it met.

The lines clash, and with a great roar across the plain
all check with the rein their horses, reared up high,
and then bear them forward of their own will. Risen into the air
the steed goes, and flying through the open ground in a swift storm
scarcely marks faint traces on the surface of the dust.
Before the rest, the swift squadron of the Boii, with Crixus their leader,
batters into the foremost and hurls its monstrous limbs against them.
He himself, swollen with pride, traced his line from the stock of ancestral Brennus,
this Crixus, and dragged the captured Capitol into his titles,
and, madman, upon his shield bore the Celts weighing out
the gold from the Tarpeian ridge and the sacred summit.
The man's milk-white neck glowed with a tawny torque,
his garments were striped with gold, his sleeves stood stiff
with gold, and his crest quivered with the like metal.
With a vast onset the foremost phalanx of the Camertes is struck down
and falls, and the close-packed waves of the Boii rush headlong
through the crowded ranks: the unspeakable Senones thicken
their allied swarms, and bodies, crushed against the breasts
of the horses, are rolled over the whole field.
The fields swim, and the deep gore of men, the deep gore of horses,
swallows the slippery footing of the warring squadron.
The heavy hoof finishes off the half-dead with its trampling,
and flying about it scatters from the blood foul dews
upon the ground, and washes the arms with the wretched men's own gore.
The first javelins, boy, of swelling Pelorus, Tyrrhenus,
dying you stain with crimson blood, victorious as they are.
For while you spur their spirits to battle with the horn
and kindle the men anew to wounds with your blast,
a barbarian weapon stuck in your panting throat
and shut up the hoarse murmur with a deadly wound.
But the sound, poured from the dying mouth at its last,
wandered through the curved horn over lips now mute.

Crixus slew Picens and Laurus, both not from afar,
but Laurus with the sword—to Picens a polished spear,
gathered on the banks of the Po, brought death. For while
he seeks the byways and plots to deceive with a leftward wheel,
the man's spear settled in his thigh and likewise through the panting
flank of the flying horse, and gave a double death, the grim thing.
The same man, wrenching from the bloody neck of Venulus,
lays you low headlong, Farfarus, with the still-warm weapon,
and you, Tullus, nursed beneath cold Velinus,
a singular glory of Ausonia and a name to be remembered,
had the fates granted delay or the Carthaginians kept their pacts;
then Remulus, and—once names most renowned in war—
the Magii of Tibur and Metaurus of Hispellum,
and Clanius, planning with wavering spear a wound.

Nor is there place for the Tyrians for war or battle, but the whole
field the Celtic frenzy has filled. The javelins fly vainly for none,
and all the steel stands fixed in a body.
Here among the trembling, daring a monstrous deed, Quirinius,
to whom flight was unknown and who chose, with unconquered mind,
in adverse straits to take death upon his breast,
fires his horse with the spur and scatters his Gallic darts from his arm,
that if a way be given to unbar a passage and to break with the steel
through to the king, sure of death he seeks in all his deeds
that glory which he could not feel. Down falls Teutalus,
his groin pierced, and the earth is shaken beneath the vast weight.
Sarmens falls, who, if victor, had vowed to lay
his yellow hair and his locks for you, Gradivus,
rivalling gold, and the ruddy knot upon his crown.
But the Fates, not hearing him vow his unshorn hair,
dragged him by it to the shades. Over his white limbs
the gore goes steaming, and the drenched earth grows red.
But Ligaunus, not slowed by the javelin that met him,
rushes in and, facing the man, wheels his sword to meet him,
and rising strikes where the sinews bind the supple arm
to the shoulder, and the right hand, cut off by the wound,
hung dying a little while from the loosened reins,
and while it gleams, with a trembling effort it grasps again the strap
and, knowing nothing, imitates one guiding the accustomed bridle.
Then Vosegus reaps the neck of the turned man, and bearing
the helmet hung up with its plume, and the enclosed face
of the slain man, hails the gods with the cry of his fathers.

And while the peoples of the Gauls give these dead to the field,
the consul, hurrying the squadrons summoned from the camp
to battle, was driving them on, and first he was rushing at the foe,
high on his gleaming white horse. He draws from every side the choice
youth of rich Ausonia, the Marsi and Cora
and the glory of Laurentum and the javelin-throwing Sabellian,
and the Mars-worshipping man of Tuder from his lofty hill,
and the Faliscans clad alike in their national linen,
and those whom, beneath Hercules' walls by the silent river,
the apple-bearing fields breed, the dwellers of the Anio by Catillus' line,
and the Hernican stones, hardened in the ice-cold streams,
and the lands of cloudy Casinum used to send.
They went into war, the nurslings of the land that rules,
a youth condemned by the gods and now never to return.
Scipio, where the central whirlpool of the fight devours the columns,
drives his horse, and, spurred by the slaughter of his own men,
slays as offerings to the dead Labarus and Padus
and Caunus and Breucus, scarcely felled by many a wound,
and Larus, who rolled his eyes with a Gorgon-like face.
You fall too, warlike Lepontius, by a grim fate;
for while, fierce, he sets his body in the way to seize the reins,
and, standing tall on foot himself, levels with the face of the seated consul,
a heavy sword fell into the middle of his brow,
and his head, split off, lay upon his shoulders. But Batus, frantic,
who wrestles with his horse and blocks the charges with his shield,
laid out on the tawny sand by a blow of the steed,
his face crushed in by the dashing heels, lost it.
The Ausonian leader rages through the troubled plains,
as the Getic North Wind, when in victory it has lifted whole
the Icarian sea from its lowest depth: the sailor is tossed,
scattered over the vast deep with his shattered fleet,
and every Cyclad is drenched by the foaming water.

Crixus, since hope was slender and salvation small,
. . .
arms his mind with contempt of death. His bristling beard
glows red with bloody foam, and the gape of the madman's mouth
whitens, and his hair is matted with the cast-up dust.
He attacks Tarius, who, the consul near, was mixing in the battles,
and thunders round the man with fierce arms.
That one rolls upon the ground; for the fir-shaft, bringing his utmost fate,
pours him forward over his horse's shoulders, and in terror
he is dragged along, his limbs bound and tangled to the girths.
Long traces of gore the spreading field leaves behind,
and the spear-point marks its quivering tracks in the dust.
The consul was praising the youth's death and making ready
to avenge those noble shades, when through his ears a dread
voice came, and he hears Crixus named by the shouting men,
though unknown to him by face. His anger rises more violent
to close fight, and he fixes his eyes on the longed-for body.
Then, urging on his horse with the welcome honour of a stroke
to its patted neck, he addresses it: "The common throng and lesser warfare
soon, Garganus: the gods call us to greater things. Do you see
how great Crixus goes? Even now I set you as your prize
that carpet shining with Sidonian flame,
a barbarian glory, and you shall be given the tawny reins."
So having spoken, with a great shout he summoned Crixus
to battle, and demanded combat in the open field.
Nor had equal anger failed to kindle the foe, who did not refuse.
When the squadrons, ordered, drew back on this side and on that
and gave room, and the fight stood in the middle of the plain,
as great as Mimas, the nursling of Earth, who in the Phlegraean fields
moved his standards and terrified heaven with his arms,
so great does Crixus from his half-bestial breast hurl forth
his roar, and rouse his wrath with horror-sounding howls:
"Has no one survived the burned and captured city,
to tell you what right hands the people of Brennus brought
to arms against you? Learn now, then," he says, and at once
hurls, with its knots and seared oak, the grim
beam, fit to shatter even the gates. It sounds with a fearful crash,
but, in its over-great cast, improvident, it saved the space
of the distant field and flies past the nearer foe.
To him the consul: "Remember to carry this to the shades and to your ancestor,
how far from the Tarpeian seat you fall, and that to you
it was not granted to look upon the Capitol of the sacred mount."
Then with knot and light running together he aids the spear,
a strain worthy of the man's bulk. It flies through the edges
of the many-fold linen and the coverings woven with sinews,
and measures the deep breast with its whole point.
He sinks down, stretched out in broad ruin upon the fields,
and the struck earth groans beneath his huge arms.
Not otherwise, on the Tyrrhenian shore, where the mole is built
to do battle against the waves and the blind storms beneath,
the lofty pier, sounding monstrously, is driven into the sea:
Nereus bellows, and the blue waters, parted by the blow,
receive beneath their angry surface the rock dashed upon them.
Their leader lost, the Celts trust themselves to flight on foot:
their one hope and all their great ardour had hung on that one life.
And as when a hunter, on the high top of Picanus,
rouses the thick coverts, and into the close lairs sends
the black plague everywhere through the bramble-tangled wilds,
while the fire gathers its silent strength and flame,
and the pitch-black summit slowly rolls in murky gloom
and twists its clouds with thick smoke:
soon the sudden blazes gleam over the whole mountain,
there is a roar, the beasts have fled, the birds have fled,
and far below in the valley the heifers tremble.

But Mago, when he sees that the squadrons have turned and that the first effort,
which alone the nation has, has come to nothing, calls to battle
the arms of his men and his nation's cavalry. From every side, bare,
they leap to the fray, both bridled and unbridled troops.
Now the Italians are borne back upon their rear with reins reversed,
now again panic carries the Tyrian squadrons backward,
or these bend their rightward circles in crescent curves,
or those wind their leftward turns into a horn-shaped sweep.
With alternating course they weave their wheeling coils
and by the same art, retreating, undo them as they yield.
With this same turn the sea, when discord stirs the winds,
the North Wind drives and the East Wind drives back, and the mass of the deep
they bear now this way, now that, with alternating gusts.

The Sidonian leader flies up, gleaming with gilded purple,
and round him Dread and Terror and Fury.
And when he raised the gleaming orb of his Callaecian shield
and struck the fields with its great light,
hope and valour fall, and from the trembling mind
the shame of turning the back recedes, nor any care for an honourable death,
but flight is fixed, and the gaping of the earth is longed for.
So, when the tigress has come forth from her Caucasian caves,
the fields are abandoned, and every flock, troubled
with maddened look, seeks safe hiding-places: she ranges
victorious over the deserted valleys, and now little by little
she bares her jaws with drawn-back gape, as if already chewing
the bodies before her, and with monstrous maw plots slaughter.
Not Metabus, not the taller Ufens
escaped her even so, though the one was borne on winged foot,
the other by his horse's help at full rein.
For the ash-spear, gleaming, sent Metabus down to the shades
with its point; Ufens, collapsed with his hamstring cut,
the sword cut off, and took with his blood the glory of his speed.
And now he had given to death Sthenius and Laurus, and from cold
Collinum Collinus, whom green Fucinus in his grotto
had nursed and given to swim across his lake.
Massicus too becomes his comrade in death, his hurled spear struck home,
begotten on the sacred summit of the vine-bearing mountain
and nursed by the waters of Liris, which with calm face
hides its course and, changing for no rain,
glides past its silent banks in a jewelled stream.

Before the front line three brothers were mingling
fierce battles, whom in Sidon, blest in her womb amid wars,
Barce had borne to Spartan Xanthippus.
Greek affairs, their father the leader, the noble name of Amyclae,
and the chains thrown on the neck of Regulus by the Spartans
swelled their hearts with old renown.
They burned to prove their race by war and their father a Laconian by their deeds,
and then to visit the cold mountains,
Taygetus, and at last, the wars subdued, to swim
their fathers' Eurotas and see the rites of Lycurgus.
But the god and the Ausonian brothers forbade them to reach
Sparta—brothers equal in number, whom harsh Aricia
had sent, born in the deep groves of Egeria,
matched in age and mind; but no further would
hard Clotho grant them to see the lake and altar of Diana.
For when, driven against their foes in the whirlwind of battle,
Eumachus and Critias and Xanthippus, glad in his father's name,
joined their steps—(as lions wage furious
wars among themselves and with panting roar
fill the squalid fields and the long native huts:
swiftly every Moor flees to the hidden rocks and trackless places,
and the Libyan wife, checking her offspring's wailing,
holds back her children from the breast;
those rage grimly, and bones broken in their bloody mouths
crunch, and limbs writhe beneath their savage teeth)—
just so the youth of Egeria, on this side keen Virbius,
on that side Capys, leap forward, and Albanus in equal arms.
Sinking down a little, Critias hurls headlong Albanus
to ruin, his belly pierced through: but to that one suddenly
the entrails, sliding in pitiable fall, filled all his shield.
Eumachus then took Capys—but he held with all his weight
the covering as though fixed to his limbs; yet the wicked sword
struck down the left hand fastened to his shield with a wound,
and, not yielding his shield though it was pressed in his own effort,
the luckless hand stuck fast among the slipping arms.
The last palm remained, two now laid low,
to Virbius. As he feigned to draw his steps in fear,
Xanthippus falls by the sword, Eumachus by the stiff spear,
and at last the fight is evened by a doubled death.
Then the blade pierced the breasts of the men in turn,
and in exchange, their lives torn away, they laid down the battle.
Happy in their death, whom love of kin added to the shades!
The coming ages will pray for such brothers,
and their glory will be eternally celebrated by a mindful age,
if only my songs have the power to carry the day
and to see late descendants, and Apollo has not begrudged them fame.

But the consul, with his voice, holds the squadrons scattering
over the whole plain, while his voice has strength: "Where do you bear back your standards?
What panic, alas, has stolen you from your own selves? If the first
bristling lot of the field seemed yours, and to provoke the battle's front,
stand behind me, men, and, your terror driven off, only
look on! These right hands that you flee were begotten by captive
fathers. What hope for the conquered? Shall we make for the Alps?
Believe that Rome herself, who bears her walls upon her tower-crowned head,
now stretches out her suppliant palms to you.
On every side I see the snatching away of children and the slaughter
of parents, and the Vestal hearths quenched with blood.
Ward off this horror!" After, amid such words, his throat
was dulled by the frequent shouting and by the thick dust,
with his left hand he seizes the reins, with his right his arms,
and thrusts forward his broad breast, and threatens with drawn sword,
now himself, now the trembling men, at close quarters, if they do not stand.

While the Father from high Olympus watches these lines,
the dangers of the noble consul moved his mind.
He calls Gradivus and thus speaks with a father's voice:
"The toil of a great-hearted man, my son—who, unless you take up the war,
will doubtless be his last—frightens me: snatch from the battle
the burning man, and forgetful of himself in his lust for slaughter,
halt the leader of Libya; for the wicked one seeks more
in the death of one consul than in the whole rout of the falling.
Besides, you see the boy who already entrusts the battle
to his tender right hand and strives to surpass his years
by his deeds and thinks it long to come to manhood through war:
let him, you his leader, dare the firstfruits of battle, you his teacher,
and let him win this first victory—to have saved his father."
So the Sower of the world. But Mars summons his chariot
to battle from the land of the Odrysians. Then he takes up
his shield that scatters the flames of the black thunderbolt,
and his helmet, easy for no god to bear, and his breastplate
sweated over with much toil of the Cyclopes,
and brandishes through the air his spear sated with blood
in the war of the Titans, and fills the fields with his car. With him
goes a host of Furies, and the Eumenides together, and the countless
shapes of bloody death, and Bellona, busied with guiding the reins,
goads the four-horse team with her black whip.
A bristling storm is borne from the boundless sky,
whirling black globes and turbid clouds,
and enfolds the earth. The Saturnian seat is shaken,
trembling at the god's coming, and the river leaves its banks
when the chariot is heard, and flows back toward its source.

The Garamantian youth had ringed the Ausonian leader with weapons
and were preparing fresh gifts for the Tyrian king,
the spoils of his arms and the consul's dripping head.
He stood resolved not to yield to Fortune, and with a fierce
mass hurled back his spears, growing more savage with the slaughter,
and now with his own, now with hostile gore, his limbs
are wet and drip, his plume is fallen, and as the ring narrows
round in its circle, the Garamantian presses with nearer javelins
and balances the iron aimed with cruel point.
Here the boy, when he saw the weapon fixed in his father's body,
his cheeks grew wet, and a sudden pallor seized the trembling
youth, and he broke out in a groan toward the stars.
Twice he had tried to forestall his father's fate,
his right hand turned against himself; twice Mars turned his wrath
upon the Carthaginians. Through the weapons, through the foe
the fearless boy is borne, and keeps pace with Gradivus' stride.
At once the squadrons gave way, and suddenly a broad
path appears across the field. Sheltered by the heavenly
shield, he reaps the ranks, and lays low upon the arms of the fallen
the bodies, and slays the author of the weapon, and many shades
before his father's eyes, the longed-for offerings.
Then, the spear quickly snatched from the hard bones,
bearing his father leaning upon his neck and shoulder,
he darts forth. The astonished squadrons, at so great a sight,
hold their weapons, and the harsh Libyan yields his place, and all
the Iberian yields far and wide, and that signal devotion and youth
wrought a wondrous silence on the warring fields.
Then from his high chariot Mars said: "You shall raze the towers
of Carthage and shall force the Tyrians to terms.
Yet in the long age no light so great shall dawn
for you, dear boy. Blessing, O blessing on your sacred nature,
true offspring of Jove. And still greater things remain,
but no better can be given." Then Mars, the clouds
and the air traversed, makes for the earth, the sun now spent,
and the darkness shut up the weary lines within their camp.

Cynthia was laying night to rest with her downward-sloping car,
fanned by her brother's wheels, and from the Eastern sea
the rosy flames were rising amid the blue.
But the consul, sad, was making for the Trebia and the hills,
fearing the plain favourable to the Carthaginians.
And now the days were snatched away in marching and busy toil,
and broken in mid-stream the bridge floated, its bonds undone,
that had carried the Dardanian column across,
when the Carthaginian came to the swift waves of Eridanus.
And while he seeks the fords and gentle approaches by winding
circuits through the byways, and looks for the languid shallows of the pool,
sometimes, the alder snatched from the neighbouring woods,
he covered the river with a fleet to carry his columns across:
behold, the consul was at hand, and held at once the borders of the Trebia,
summoned through the long blue sea past Sicilian Pelorus,
the offspring of the Gracchi. A clan famous for a great
and spirited man, and many an ancestor among the images
shone forth with bright titles in war and at home.
Nor were the Carthaginians wanting, their camp pitched across the river
on the grass. For prosperity stirred their spirits,
and their leader, taunting them besides: "What third consul
now remains to the city? What other Sicania remains
under arms? See, all the bands of the Latins and of the grandsons
of Daunus have come together. Let them now strike treaties with me,
the leaders of Italy, and demand back laws and pacts.
But you, granted your weapons amid the light of war,
unhappy in soul, so, so may you live, and to your son
once more give this glory; nor in the close of your age
be it granted to meet death in war, when the fates shall call.
To have fallen fighting is my privilege." Thus he loudly proclaims, ablaze.
Then with a light javelin, busy, with his Massylian squadrons
he provokes them beneath the very camp and draws out the foe.
Nor does the Latin soldier think it right to owe his safety
to the rampart, or that the closed gates be battered by the spear.
They burst out, and before all flies over the open mound
a consul in no way unworthy of the Gracchi. The breeze shakes the waving
crests of his Auruncan helmet, and from his shoulder gleams
the ancestral glory of his blood-red cloak. With a great
shout he calls his columns back, and where the crowd, meeting him,
packs its dense ranks, breaking a path he is borne across the field,
as a torrent, headlong from the top of lofty Pindus,
rushes with a roar into the plains and with a great crash
rolls a side torn from the mountain: everywhere, meeting it,
the herds and the monstrous beasts and the woods are dragged along,
and the foaming wave shouts in the rocky valleys.

Not if the glory of the Maeonian tongue should return to me,
and Father Phoebus should grant me to pour forth a hundred voices,
could I tell over all the slaughters that the right hand of the great
consul, or against him the frenzy of Tyrian wrath, brought forth.
Murranus by the leader of Libya, and the leader of the Phalanti
by the Ausonian—men skilled in war and old in toil—
each laid low the other's, face to face.
Murranus stormy Anxur had sent from its mountain,
you, Phalantus, the rites sacred to Triton from the snow-white deep.
As soon as the consul shone in his splendid raiment,
though deprived of part of his sight, with one eye Cupencus,
sufficing for the wars, fiercely brandishes his spear
and fixes it quivering on the margin of the topmost shield.
To him the consul (for anger boils him): "Lay down, wicked one, whatever
remains in your fierce face and gleams on your maimed brow."
So he says, hurling with a straight whirl the oaken shaft,
and sends the grim light through with his whole point.
Nor more lightly does the son of Hamilcar rage on his right.
To him falls luckless Varenus in his snow-white armour,
Varenus of Mevania, for whom the rich teat of the field
Fulginia ploughs, and Clitumnus in the broad meadows
washes his white bulls in his cold stream.
But the gods are grim, and that greatest care, a victim
thankless, was reared in vain for the Tarpeian Thunderer.
The light Iberian presses on, and lighter the Moor to range about.
On this side javelins, on that the Libyan cornel-spears strive
to weave the sky with a dense cloud, and as much of the level field
as lies between to the banks, so much do the quivering
weapons bury, and there is no room in death for the crowded to fall.
Allius, set out from Argyripa and the fields of Daunus,
a hunter, was ranging over the plain with rough javelins
and his Iapygian horse, and borne into the midst of the foe,
hurled his Apulian darts with no idle right hand.
For him a breastplate bristles with the hide of a Samnite she-bear,
and his helmet is fenced with the tusks of an aged boar.
But when, as he wrought havoc, as though over the open he ranged the lairs
in a wood, or stirred up the backs of beasts on Garganus,
on this side Mago, on that as savage saw him likewise Maharbal,
as when, with hunger driving them, two bears from opposite crags
attack a frightened bull between their twin onslaughts,
and rage suffers no sharing of the prey, just so the keen
Allius is brought down, his javelin hurled from this side and that:
the Moorish yew goes whistling through both flanks.
Then the meeting points sounded in the midst of his heart,
and it was uncertain to which spear his death should yield.
And now, the standards scattered, through the Roman ranks
the Carthaginian drives the stragglers to the banks—a pitiable thing—
pressing the panicked men and striving to plunge them in the river.
Then the Trebia begins new battles in its ill-omened flood
for the weary, and rouses its waves by the prayers of Juno.
The sinking earth swallows the bodies of the fleeing
and, treacherous in its soil, sucks them down in its baffling gulf.
Nor is it given to strive and to wrench from the sticky mud
the steps sunk deep within: by the tenacious slime
the bound footsteps cling fast, and the loosened bank
entangles, or with the blind treachery of the marsh strikes them down.
And now one over another, rising up through the slippery places,
while each man snatches a way for himself over the inextricable
shore, and struggles with the rotten turf, slipping
they fall and crush themselves with their own ruin.
That swift swimmer, now just about to grasp safety,
while he makes ready and, straining with lifted body, grasps
the topmost grass with his hand and emerges from the liquid waves,
hangs pinned by a spear hurled into the bank.
Here one, robbed of his weapon, clasps the foe with his arms
and, mingling death, holds him fast struggling in the shallows.
A thousand shapes of death at once. The Ligurian falls in the fields,
but the man's face, cast into the river waters,
drank in long gasps the bloody stream.
At last fair Irpinus was barely swimming out from the mid-flood
and calling his comrades' hands with a shout,
when a fierce horse, carried by the swift waters and with many a wound,
struck him and sank the weary man beneath the surface.
Disaster is heaped up by a force of elephants, suddenly seen
across the waters, urged on with their turreted backs.
For it is swept headlong through the shallows, like a crag torn down
from a rent mountain, and drives before its breast the Trebia,
which fears the strange thing, and lies upon the foaming channel.
Adversity tests men, and through hardship up the steep cliff
fearless valour strives toward glory.
For Fibrenus, unable to bear losing his death unhonoured
and bare of fame, "We shall be marked," he said,
"nor, Fortune, will you hide my death beneath the flood.
I will try whether there is on earth what the Ausonian sword
cannot tame, or the Tyrrhenian spear cannot pierce through."
Then rising he casts, and plants in the right eye
of the beast his cruel javelins, and leaves the weapon in the wound.
With a horror-sounding shriek the monster follows
the penetrating thrust of the point, and, mangled, with gore poured forth,
lifts its brow and, its driver fallen, turns its back.
Then in truth they attack with javelins and frequent arrow,
daring now to hope for its death, and through the huge shoulders
and the stretched-out flanks the wound comes with its black point.
Many a lance stands in its back and on its dark spine,
and it brandishes a vast forest with its shaken body,
until, the weapons spent in the long contest,
it falls and closes the shallows it presses with its great ruin.

Behold, against the stream, though his slowed limbs
are held back by a man's wound, the implacable Scipio
goes up the river and harasses the foe with countless slaughters.
With the bodies and shields and helmets at once of the fallen
the Trebia is covered, and one is scarcely left to see the waves.
Mazaeus by javelin, Gestar is laid low by sword,
then Thelgon, dweller of Cyrene, with a Pelopid ancestor.
At him he hurls a pike caught up from the swift flood,
and as far as the point, drawn thin by its long stiff iron,
projects, he drives it through the gaping mouth.
Struck by the wood, the teeth sounded in the wound.
Nor was rest sought in death: his swelling limbs
the Trebia gave to Eridanus, Eridanus to the waters of the sea.
You too, Thapsus, fall, a tomb denied you after death.
What did the house of the Hesperides or the groves of the goddesses avail,
guarding the tawny boughs on the gold-bearing tree?

The Trebia swelled and raised itself from its deepest pools,
and now, fierce, drives forth its whole spring in a flood
and hurls all its force. The wave rages with sounding
eddies, and a new torrent follows with a roar.
The leader felt it, and with kindled anger more violently:
"Great penalties, O Trebia, and deserved, will you pay
to me, treacherous one," he said: "torn through the Gallic
streams I will scatter you over the fields, and take from you the name of river,
and stop up the very spring from which you open, nor shall it be granted you
to touch your banks and glide into the Po. What sudden madness
has made you, unhappy, a Sidonian river?"
As he hurls such words, a rising mound of waters
struck him and pressed his shoulders with its curved flood.
Steep against the opposing mass of the rushing waves
the leader stands, and lifted on his shield the rushing river.
Moreover, from behind, the foaming wave with a whistling storm
sprinkles his topmost crest with spray.
To go through the shallows and to set a firm step the god forbids,
the earth withdrawn beneath him, and far off the struck
rocks sound hoarsely, and the waves, roused to the wars of their parent,
do battle, and the river has lost its banks.
Then, his hair wet and bound with sea-green leaves,
he lifts up his head with a voice: "Do you threaten besides
to wipe out my proud penalties and the name of Trebia,
O foe to my realms? How many bodies I carry,
laid low by your right hand! By the shields and helmets of the men
you slay, my course and channel are narrowed and choked.
With slaughter, you see, my deep pools redden and are borne backward.
Set a limit to your right hand, or fall upon the neighbouring fields."

These things, Venus joined to her, from a high mound was watching
Mulciber, hidden in the gloom of a dark cloud,
and Scipio, his palms lifted, presses heavy toward heaven:
"Gods of my fathers, by whose auspices Dardan Rome stands,
did you save me of late from such a death amid so great a battle?
Was it thought unworthy that this life be cut off by a brave
right hand? Give me back, O son, to dangers,
give me back to the foe! Let it be allowed me, in battle, to summon a death
that I may approve to my country and my brother." Then, stirred by his words,
Venus groaned and turned upon the river the swift
might of her unconquered husband. The scattered fire drives flames
on every side along the banks, and burning lays waste
the shades nursed for many years by the river.
The whole grove burns, and Vulcan, poured into the high woods
in victory, crackles with loosened reins.
And now the fir is scorched in its foliage, now the pine and the alders,
now the poplar, standing on its bare trunk alone, has let fall on high
the birds wont to dwell among its branches.
The greedy flame drinks up the waters drawn from the deepest
flood, and, the savage heat pressing on,
the dry gore parches on the banks. Far and wide the bristling
earth is split into cracks and gapes, broken open with a chasm,
and on the pools the deep ashes have settled.

Father Eridanus marvels that his eternal courses
suddenly cease, and the mourning choir of the Nymphs filled
their innermost caves with stunned wailing.
Three times, as he tried to lift his scorched head, Vulcan
plunged it back beneath the smoking waves with hurled torch,
three times the seized reed bared the god's hair.
Then at last his voice was admitted and the vows of one who prayed,
and to him praying it was granted to keep his former banks,
and at last from the Trebia Scipio called back his weary
cohorts to a fortified hill, with Gracchus attending.
But the Carthaginian, having venerated the river with much honour,
set up grassy altars by its allied waters,
not knowing, alas, what greater things the gods were stirring,
and what grief, Trasimene, you were preparing for Ausonia.

The peoples of the Boii had Flaminius lately disturbed
with arms, and to that man the glory of war was then easy,
to crush a nation light in heart and poor in cunning.
But it was no equal task to have contended with the Tyrian tyrant.
This man, born for the city's fatal harm by left-hand
omens, the Saturnian prepares for the weary empire
as a leader, and a man worthy of the coming ruin.
Then, when the first day of his office and the helm of the country
to be guided he seized, and the camp was under his command,
as one untaught of the sea and ignorant to handle
the deep by art, if he has taken charge of a wretched ship,
holds himself the place of the winds, and to every storm
gives the vessel to be tossed: the ship is borne wandering on the flood
onto the rocks, his own right hand, the helmsman's, driving it—
so the army is driven headlong, its arms snatched up,
against the peoples of the Lydians and the seat consecrated of old
from the origin of ancient Corythus, and the Maeonian
colonists joined by the blood of their ancestors to the Italians, their stock intermingled.

Nor does the warning god delay the king of the Africans from his task,
worth such great praise. Sleep had hidden all things
and was giving forgetfulness to their anxious cares,
when Juno, changed into the deity of the neighbouring pool
and her wet brow girt with poplar leaves,
stirs his heart with sudden cares
and breaks the leader's rest with a voice not to be scorned:
"O Hannibal, happy in fame and a name to be wept by Latium,
if Fortune had created you for Ausonia,
destined for the great gods—why do we hold back the fates?
Drive off delay. Brief is the Fortune of great favour.
As much as you vowed, when you swore the Dardan wars
to your father, so much blood from an Ausonian body
shall flow for you, and you shall sate your father's shades with slaughter.
To us you shall pay your due honours, free of care.
For I am that one whom, ringed with lofty mountains,
the band sent from Tmolus surrounds—Trasimene of the shady pools."
By these warnings he is moved, and the youth, glad in the deity,
he straightway carries headlong over the ridge of the airy mountain.
Apennine bristled with ice among the slippery rocks,
mingling its pine-bearing head with the highest sky.
The deep snow had hidden the timber, and on the lofty peak
the hoary crest rose to the stars with crusted frost.
He bids them go. Sooner does his glory seem to be quenched and to fall,
if a stand be made at any mountains after the Alps.
They climb the cloudy summits of the sheer crag.
Nor does the conquering of the ridge end or soothe their toil:
the flats swim, and with rotten ice in the melting waters
the trackless fields stand flooded in a miry swamp.
And now the leader's bare crown, amid such inhospitable places,
is shaken by the cruelty of the sky, while down his face
and his cheeks the eye runs. Easy is it to scorn the healers:
he believes the longed-for time for war well bought
at whatever peril. He spares not the honour of his face,
provided he lose not his march, nor does he hesitate to give his other limbs
as the price of war, if victory demand it,
and he thinks it light enough to see the Capitol as victor,
where to make for it and where to strike the Italian foe at close quarters.
Having endured such things, at last among the savagery of the place
they came to the longed-for lakes, where then in arms
he would take ample atonement for his lost sight.

But behold, the senators were at hand, sent from Carthage.
No small cause for the journey, nor glad were the tidings they brought.
It was the custom among the peoples whom the stranger Dido founded,
to seek the gods' favour with slaughter, and upon the blazing altars
(unspeakable to tell) to place little children.
The yearly urn brought back the pitiable lots,
its rites imitating the sacred ways of Thoantean Diana.
For him the discordant Hanno, of old hostile, by the custom
of the gods sought out, by lot and fate, the offspring of Hannibal.
But a nearer fear was from the wrath of the armed leader,
and great before their eyes stood the image of his return.
This Imilce makes harsher, her cheeks befouled and her hair torn,
and fills the city with the clamour of her grief,
as an Edonian woman on Pangaeus, stirred by the triennial rite,
goes over the ridges and sighs within her breast for the enclosed Bacchus.
So among the Tyrian mothers, as if set beneath the torches,
she cries: "Ah, husband, in whatever quarter of the world
you wage your wars, hither bear your standards. More violent is the foe here,
here nearer. You now perhaps beneath the very
walls of the Dardan city receive the quivering weapons
upon your shield, unafraid, and brandishing the savage
torch, carry fires to the Tarpeian roofs.
Meanwhile your first home and only offspring,
alas, in the bosom of his fatherland, is dragged to the Stygian altars.
Go now, lay waste with the sword the Ausonian household gods
and toil at forbidden roads. Go, unseal the pacts
sworn by all the gods. So Carthage repays
your rewards and even now pays you such honours.
And further, what piety is this, to sprinkle the shrines with gore?
Alas, the first causes of crime to wretched mortals,
not to know the nature of the gods! Go, pray for what is just
with pious incense, and turn away the cruel rites of slaughter.
Gentle and akin to man is god. Thus far, I pray,
let it be enough to have seen bullocks slain before the altars.
Or if the gods wish the unspeakable, and it is fixed and settled,
me, me, who bore him, consume with your vows.
Why does it please to despoil the Libyan lands of this offspring?
Or were the Aegates more to be wept, and the Punic realms
sunk in the deep, if once, by bloody lot,
so great a valour of my husband had been snatched away beforehand?"
These words, in their wavering fear of gods and man alike,
drew the senators to caution, and left it to him
whether to refuse the lot or obey the gods' honour.
Then indeed Imilce trembled with fear, scarce mistress of herself,
dreading the harsh heart of her great-souled husband.
Hearing this eagerly, the leader thus then speaks:
"What, equalled to the gods, can Hannibal pay you
not unequal to so great a gift? What rewards worthy of you
shall I find, mother Carthage? Night and day
I will bear arms, and from here I will make many a
noble victim come from Ausonian Quirinus to your temples.
But the boy, the heir of arms and war, shall be saved.
Hope, O son, of mine and sole salvation of Tyrian affairs,
while Hesperia threatens, remember to contend
with the sons of Aeneas by land and sea, while life shall stand.
Go on (the Alps lie open) and press on at my toil.
You also, gods of my fathers, whose shrines are appeased
with slaughter and who delight to be worshipped by the dread of mothers,
turn hither your glad faces and your whole minds.
For I prepare rites and toil at greater altars.
You, Mago, take your stand on the top of the mountain opposite;
you, Choaspes, draw nearer to the leftward hills;
let Sychaeus lead through the dark places to the barriers and the gorge.
But I, Trasimene, with my roving soldiery, headlong
will range you over, and seek from the gods the offerings of war.
For the god promises in no small things by open pledges
which, once seen, men, you may carry back to your native city."

9. Latium being troubled by portents, and the gods revealing
through Ausonia the unavailing signs of the disaster to come,
no otherwise than if the omens of the battle to come were favourable
and prosperous, the consul passed the night
sleepless and brandished his weapon in his hand through the shadows,
and now upbraided Paulus for sloth, now made the keen
trumpets sound and longed for the war-call of the night.
Nor was the ardour for a hasty contest less in the Carthaginian.
They burst from the rampart, the sinister Fortune urging them on,
and hands were joined. For the Macae, scattered through the neighbouring
fields to snatch up fodder, poured forth a flying
cloud of weapons. Foremost of all to invade the war,
Mancinus, glad, and first to dye his weapons
with the enemy's blood, falls, and the numerous youth falls.
Nor would Varro have curbed the arms, with the god rebuking him
by the entrails of the beasts and the auspices opposed to Paulus,
had not the lot of the alternate command, by which the camp is ruled,
denied to him, hastening to his fate, the decision of battle.
Yet this availed to grant to the thousands that were to perish
no more than a single day. They returned to the camp, while Paulus
groaned without doubt, who saw that tomorrow's authority
would yield to the madman, and that in vain his men's
lives had been preserved from slaughter. For, turbid with anger
and hostile to delay because of the battle put off, the leader:
'Is it thus, thus,' he said, 'Paulus, that you repay thanks and reward
for your own life? Did they deserve such things, who tore you
from the laws and the urn that menaced you with doom?
Nay, let them at once hand over to the enemy their recalled swords,
let them hand over their arms, command it, or strip them from the right hands of those who fight.
But you, whose eyes and faces I saw wet,
when the consul bade you turn your backs and return,
wait not for the wonted signal of battle to be sought.
Let each, his own leader, snatch his way, when Phoebus
shall begin to sprinkle with his first rays the Gargan summits.
I myself will open the gates in haste. Rush more swiftly, and recall
this day that was snatched from you.' So, turbid, he set the sick
camp ablaze with a deadly love of battle.

But Paulus, now no longer the same in mind or face,
but such as he stood after the battle, on plains strewn
with the soldiery destroyed, with the coming evil hovering
before his eyes and face, as when, the hope of light now taken away,
a lifeless mother is stunned and warms in vain with last
embraces the limbs of her son still warm:
'By the walls of Rome so often shaken,' he said,
'and by these innocent souls, around which the night now flies
with its Stygian shade, spare to go against the disaster.
While the gods' frenzy passes and the anger of Fortune is spent,
the strangeness of Hannibal is enough, if the soldier
learns to bear the name, and looks on the foe without growing cold.
Do you not see, when he is heard of in the neighbouring fields,
how suddenly the blood leaves the pale bodies,
and how the arms fall before the trumpets? The delayer and, as you think,
the feeble Fabius, however many he led into battle
beneath those censured standards, now they take up arms.
But those whom Flaminius—but the gods avert the dire omen.
But if your spirit fights against our warnings and prayers,
open your ears to the god. The Cumaean prophetess sang
these things once through the world, and, foretelling, made known to the lands
your frenzies and yours, in the age of our forefathers.
And now a second prophet to you, in no riddling song, before your face
I sing the fates: if you do not halt tomorrow's standards,
you will confirm with our blood the words of the Phoebean
Sibyl. Nor hereafter shall the fields be made famous by Greek
Diomedes, but, if you persist, by you the consul.'
So Paulus, and tears rose in his burning eyes.

The night too a wicked error defiled.
Satricus, captured by Xanthippus, had endured slavery
on the Libyan shores, and soon among the prizes was given
as a gift to the king of the Autololes for the honour of his valour.
He had a home and twin sons, left behind at Sulmo
at their mother's breast, Mancinus and, together,
Solimus of Rhoetean name. For his stock was Dardanian
and his race from a Phrygian forefather, who, following the sceptre
of Aeneas, had founded a city famous for its walls,
called Solimon after himself. Soon, celebrated by the Italian
colonists, by degrees the name worn down to Sulmo.
But then Satricus, brought with the king amid barbarian troops,
who was not despised, if need required it,
to teach the Gaetulians Latin words as interpreter,
after it was granted him that he might revisit his Pelignian dwelling
and hope for his native hearth, calls the night to his attempt
and stealthily escapes from the unkind camp.
But the man's flight was bare. For, taking up a shield, he avoided
betraying his enterprise, and was returning with his right hand unarmed.
The spoils therefore and the bodies laid low on the field
he searches, and girds himself with the stripped arms of Mancinus.
And now his fear was lighter. But he from whom he bore the spoils
torn from the lifeless one, and whose limbs he had stripped,
was his own son, laid low a little before by the Macan foe.

Behold, at the coming of night and the first slumber,
the other of his sons, Solimus, had carried his steps,
wakeful, over the Ausonian rampart, while by lot in turn
he changed the watches at the gate, and was seeking among the scattered
dead the body of his brother Mancinus, laid low,
desiring to lay the wretched one in stealthy earth.
Nor had he hastened far on his way, when he sees the foe
coming in arms toward the Sidonian mound,
and, with what chance gave unforeseen in sudden straits, in the tomb
of Aetolian Thoas he hides his concealed limbs.
Then, when he sees no arms following more closely behind, and the man
bearing his unaccompanied steps through the shadows,
springing from the mound he hurls his bare javelin
not in vain into his father's back, and Satricus, believing
the band that followed to be Tyrian and the wounds Sidonian,
trembling, looks about for the author of the blind blow.
But when his course brought the victor near with youthful strength,
and the grim light flashed from the familiar arms,
and his brother's shield from afar, the moon betraying it, uncovered
itself before his eyes and the boss gleamed close at hand,
the youth cries out, set ablaze by sudden anger:
'May I not be your offspring, Satricus, born at Sulmo,
nor your brother, Mancinus, and may I confess myself a descendant
unworthy of Pergamean Solimus, if it be granted this man
to escape my hands unpunished. Shall you bear the noble
spoil of my brother before my eyes and carry back, treacherous,
while I breathe, the proud arms of the Pelignian house?
These gifts, dear mother Acca, for the comfort of your grief
I will bring you, to fix forever on your son's tomb.'
Crying out such things, with drawn sword he rushed on.
But from the other now the weapons, now the arms slipped from his hand
when he heard his country and his sons and his wife and the arms named,
and a cold horror had stunned his limbs and his senses.
Then a pitiable voice is poured from his half-dead mouth:
'Spare, I pray, your right hand—not that life may remain to me
(for it is a sin to wish to enjoy this), but with our blood
do not condemn your hands, O son. That captive of Carthage,
now first brought to his native shores,
I am that Satricus, of Solimus's stock. No guilt, my son,
is yours. When you hurled the spear, hot, against me,
I was a Carthaginian. But, escaped from the bitter camp,
I was hastening to you and to the face of my dear wife:
this shield I snatched from the lifeless one. But now, my only one,
carry these arms, excused, back to your brother's tomb.
Yet let it be your first care, son, to bear back
to the leader Paulus the warning: let him strive to draw out the war
and refuse the contests of Mars to the Carthaginian.
He exults in the gods' augury and hopes for measureless
slaughter in the near battle. I beg, restrain the raging
Varro: for the report is that he urges on the standards.
Great enough at this turning-point of my wretched life will be
this solace, to have provided for my own. Now, son, give
to a father found and lost at once the last
kisses.' So speaking, he takes off his helmet and seizes the neck
of his stiffened son with trembling arms:
he labours to heal with words the shame of his son, stunned in mind,
for the wound he has dealt, and to excuse the weapon:
'What witness, what accomplice was present at our deeds?
Did not the night hide the error with its blackening shade?
Why do you tremble? Give, son, give more, give me to join breast to breast.
I, the father myself, absolve your hand, and at the end of my labours
close my eyes with this right hand, I beg.' But the wretched youth,
sighing from the depth of his breast, returns no words or response
to the address, nor any voice, but hastens to stop
the course of the black blood and, weeping, to bind more swiftly
the deep wound with a torn covering.
At last amid his groans the wretched laments broke forth:
'Is it thus, father, that Fortune brings you back to us
in our country? Thus, impious, does she restore you to your son
and your son to his father? O thrice and four times happy
brother, to whom it was given by the fates to recognize his father lost.
But I, unslain by the Sidonians, behold, by my father's
wound recognize my father. Would that at least this, Fortune, had been
a solace for my fault, that you had given me doubtful signs
of my ill-omened race. But it shall be left to the unjust
gods no longer to make our labours criminal.'
While, distraught, he laments these things, now, the blood failing,
the old man had scattered his life into the empty air.
Then the youth, raising his sorrowful face to the stars:
'Witness, daughter of Titan, of my polluted right hand and of the unspeakable
deed, who by your nocturnal light directed my weapons
into my father's body, no longer,' he said,
'shall you be defiled by these eyes and their condemned sight.'
This he says, and at once digs his sword into his breast and, holding up
the black wound, with the flowing blood marks
on the shield his father's charge: FLEE THE BATTLE, VARRO,
and hangs the covering on the point of his uplifted spear
and stretches his limbs over his lamented father.

Such omens of the battle to come the gods were sending
to the Ausonians, and, the shades by degrees departing,
the night, conscious of the crime, yielded to the rosy Dawn.
The Libyan leader called his men to arms, and the Roman to arms
called his after the custom, and for the Carthaginians there returned
a day such as none had ever risen in all the ages.

'You have no need,' said the Carthaginian, 'of goading words,
who from the Herculean pillars to the fields of Iapyx
have measured the road by conquering. Nowhere is spirited Saguntum,
the Alps have yielded, the very proud father of Ausonian waters,
Eridanus, flows down in a captive channel.
The Trebia is sunk with the slaughter of men, and the Lydian mouths
are pressed by Flaminius's tomb, and far and wide the fields
gleam with bones and are furrowed by no ploughshare.
A more illustrious title and a light that will bring more blood
rises. To me, greatness enough, indeed enough and more
than enough be the reward of war: let the rest be conquered
by you. Whatever Rome carried down from the rich Spaniard,
whatever she paraded in her Aetnean triumphs,
nay even whatever, snatched from the Libyan shore,
she stored away, shall come to your swords without casting lots.
Carry home what the right hand shall give. I, your leader, ask
no honour from the spoils. Through the long ages the Dardanian
plunderer shall have stripped for you the world that is now subdued.
You who draw your Sarranian name from a Tyrian origin,
whether the Laurentine land, furrowed by the Sigean farmer,
smiles on you, or whether the Byzacian fields are dearer
to your heart, sprouting with a hundred stalks for Ceres,
I will grant you to choose select fields among the prizes.
I will add too the banks which the Tiber waters with its yellow wave,
to graze far and wide with captive flocks.
But you who, an ally of foreign blood, move my standards
of Byrsa, if you raise a right hand red with Ausonian
slaughter, be from this moment a citizen of Carthage.
And let not Garganus and the shores of Daunus deceive you:
you stand at the walls of Rome. Though the trackless city
is far off and stands distant from our contest,
here today she falls, and beyond this I summon no soldier
to battle: from the battle-line make your course to the Capitol.'
This he says. Then, the defence of the rampart driven forward,
they snatched away the delays of the ditches, and his battle-line
he fits with skill to the place, in order, on the curving banks.
On the left wing for the contest stood the barbarian
warrior Nasamon, and with him the Marmarid, huger of limb,
then the fierce Moor and the Garamantian and the Macae
and the Massylian lines and the throng of the Adyrmachidae,
glad to live by the sword, the people dwelling beside the Nile,
keeping their bodies blackened by the excessive sun.
Their head set over the columns and their command was Nealces.
But on the right, where the Aufidus curves its wave with windings
and wanders around its banks with curving eddy,
Mago rules. The light troops came up whom bristling
Pyrene sent, the peoples, and girded with varied tumult
the river's side: the light-shielded youth gleams,
the Cantabrian before the rest, and the Vasco, his temples uncovered,
and the Balearic, mingling battles with whirled lead,
and the men sprung from the Baetis. Lofty in the centre, he himself
controls the columns, which he strengthened with native soldiery and which
with the troops of the Celts, often steeped in the Eridanus.
But where the river, with its waters slipping back,
withdraws itself and walls the wedges with no defence,
the beast, bearing on its black back turreted masses
and bulwarks, like a moving mound,
nods and lifts up its high walls to the air.
The rest it is granted now to the Numidians, to fly around
and bear their wandering courses and to seethe over the whole field.

While the Libyan, his soldiery kindled, dispenses his forces,
and, insatiable, again and again by exhorting urges
each man by his own deeds, and boasts that he knows
from what right hand come the hissings of the shrieking weapon,
and promises the men that he will fail none as witness,
already Varro, the legion led out of the rampart, was setting in motion
the beginnings of disaster, and, glad, the ferryman over the pale
wave was making room for the shades to come.
The foremost stand still, whom the bloody mark hanging
on the shield forbade to go, and, fixed by the omen, they grow numb.
Beside them a terrible sight: pitiable lay
the bodies in an embrace, and the son, his right hand
laid on his father's breast, covered the deadly wound.
Tears flowed, and thence the grief of Mancinus, brought back
in his brother's death, then the sad augury moved them,
and the face, like a dead man's, on the lifeless body.
Swiftly the fault of the error and the deeds to be lamented
they unfold to the leader, and the arms forbidding battle.
He, burning in spirit: 'Bear all this,' he said, 'to Paulus.
For him, in whose womanish heart fears stand,
that hand may move, which, steeped in unspeakable slaughter,
when the Furies sought their penalties, perhaps with his father's
blood, as he died, sealed the wicked verse.'
Then, threatening, in haste he distributes the duties of battle,
and where Nealces, savage, marshals the wild nations and his line,
there he opposes himself with the Marsian soldiery and against
the standards of the Samnites and the Iapygian nursling.
But in the middle of the field (for in this part he saw
the leader of Libya stand) Servilius is bidden to go to meet
the arms and to lead on the Picentes and the Umbrians.
The rest of the contests Paulus holds on the right wing.
Above these, to go against the ambushes and the flying band
of the Numidians is granted to the son of Scipio, and he foretells
that the squadrons which by craft and tricks will split themselves
he is to scatter the war among.

And now the battle-lines drew near, and with the nimble running
of men and with mouths made hot at once by the mingled
neighing of the hoofed beasts and the much-clashing arms
a blind murmur wandered through the troubled columns.
So, when the winds first stir contests on the sea,
the wave of the strait brings to birth the rage shut within
and the storms that will scatter the stars, and, moved from its depths,
breathes through the rocks the threatening sounds, and, driven from its caverns,
whirls the panting sea with foaming eddy.
Nor indeed was that toil, in so savage a whirlwind of fate,
of the lands alone. Mad discord
entered heaven and forced the gods to war.
On this side Mavors, on this Apollo, the companion of Gradivus,
and the tamer of the swollen sea fights, on this Venus, distraught,
on this Vesta and, stirred by the slaughter of captured Saguntum,
the son of Amphitryon, and likewise venerable Cybele
and the Indigetes gods and Faunus and the founder Quirinus
and Pollux, alternating his soul with Castor exchanged.
Against them, her side girt with iron, Saturnian Juno
and Pallas, born of the Tritonian's Libyan waters,
and ancestral Hammon, his horns bent over his temples,
and a great throng besides of the lesser gods.
When at the mass of them coming together and at their steps the kindly
earth trembled, part filled the neighbouring mountains,
divided, part took their seat beneath a high cloud:
the descent to battle was made through the empty sky.

A measureless shout is raised to the deserted stars,
as great as the voices the earth-born army poured to the air
on the Phlegraean plains, or as the new thunderbolts
Jupiter, the sower of the ages, demanded of the Cyclopes with great voice,
when he saw the great-souled Giants go, with mountains heaped up,
to seize the heavenly realms.
Nor indeed in such great clashes was there any
first spear: a shrieking cloud, with the rage of weapons
contending, was poured forth at once, and the souls, greedy
of blood, fell on this side and that in a twin storm.
And before the mad sword is drawn by the right hand,
a great part of the fighters lies low. Over the very bodies
of their own they stand, eager, and trample on the groaning.
And no more can the Dardanian manhood be thrust forth
or turned away by the Libyan effort, nor can the Sarranian band,
fixed in its rank, be driven, than if the sea
should begin to tear Calpe from its seat with its hurled flood.
They have lost the room for a blow, nor, with death accomplished,
can they fall, hemmed in. The helmet, grim, blazes
at the clash of the opposing helmet, and the shield gapes
at the push of a shield, and sword is bruised by sword.
Foot is worn by foot, and man by man, and the earth cannot
be seen, covered with blood, and a dense night, hanging
beneath the air with weapons heaped on, took away the sky and the stars.
Those whom Fortune had granted to stand in a favourable place
with the long blow of the pike and the tall point,
as if they drove the front lines, mingle their contests.
But those whom an inglorious rank holds behind,
strive with missiles to equal the battles of those before them.
Beyond, the shout drives the war, and the soldier, lacking
the Mars he longs for, urges on the foe with savage cries.
No kind of weapon is wanting. These rouse battles
with the stake, these with the blazing pine, these with the weight of the javelin,
but another with stones and the sling and the flying dart.
At times the shrieking reed is borne through the clouds,
at times the firebrand-spear, to be feared by the very walls.

Do we hope, goddesses, whose sacred rites are tended by me,
that we can open out this whole day, with a mortal voice,
to the ages? Do you grant me so much to trust to my tongue
that I should sound Cannae with one mouth? If our glory
pleases you and you do not turn away from great daring,
hither summon all song and Phoebus the father.
But would, henceforth, Roman, that you might bear favouring fortune
in such spirit as you now bear adverse, and let them be, I pray, thus far,
nor let it please the gods to try whether the Trojan offspring
can endure an equal war. And you, anxious for your fate,
lay aside, I beg, your tears, and worship the wounds that will bring you
perpetual praises. For at no time, Rome,
will you be greater. Soon you will so slip in prosperity
that you preserve by fame the names of your disasters alone.

And now Fortune, alternating among the various changes
of fortune on both sides, had mocked their angers with an uncertain
outcome, and, with the hope of both nations long hanging in the midst,
Mavors blazed amid the matched arms:
as when gentle breezes stir the green stalks,
and the wind does not yet drive the ears that are not yet ripe,
hither and thither the top of the crop goes, and, nodding in turn
with alternate motion, gleams, slowly bent.
At last Nealces, charging with a sharp shout, scatters the line
broken by the barbarian forces.
The wedges were loosened, and through the gaps, hastened on,
the foe burst upon the alarmed. Then in a black whirlwind
a torrent of blood overflows, and no body falls
beneath a single point. While the Ausonian warrior
fears wounds in the back, he catches the savage deaths
in his breast and wards off disgrace from his death.

There stood among the foremost in the contest of the middle battle,
ever loving the harsh and equal to any peril,
Scaevola, and now he did not wish for life amid so great a slaughter,
but a death worthy of his forefather and a dying under a name.
He, after he saw that things were broken and that destruction
grew, said: 'Let us extend whatever brief space of life is left;
for valour is an idle name,
unless the times of a glorious death be enough in the bearing.'
He spoke, and into the midst, where the roused right hand of the Carthaginian
drives a path, straining, he is borne with a vast whirlwind.
Here he comes upon Caralis, exulting and wishing to put on
the snatched gear from a slain man's lofty trunk,
with his sword, and drove the iron in, in anger, up to the hilt.
That man rolls, falling, and at the hostile fields with his bite
he snatches and presses the pangs of death into the earth.
Nor did the raging hands of Gabar and Siccha hold back
their man with united valour; but keen Gabar lost,
while he stood, his right hand, cut off amid the battles;
and Siccha, while, with great grief troubling him,
he rashly hastens aid, unforeseeing trod on a sword
and fell, and too late condemned the steps of his bare
foot, and lies by the right hand of his dying friend.
At last the swelling fury of the youth turned the fatal weapons
of lightning-like Nealces. He leaps forth, burning,
with so famous a name goading him toward the prizes of slaughter.
Then a flint, torn from a crag, which the torrent had brought down
from the high mountains, he snatches and, turbid, whirls into his face.
The jaws cracked at the dashed weight,
and the face was carried away from the man: the gore
flows through the nostrils with the bloody brain congealed, and black
the eyes drip from their crushed sockets and the maimed lights from the forehead.
Marius is laid low, having tried to succour his like-souled
Caper, and fearing to survive the man as he fell.
The same beginning of life, the same fatherland, and common to the two
their poverty: the youths, born at sacred Praeneste,
had mingled their pursuits and sowed on shared land.
The same was their to-wish and not-to-wish, and a mind allied
through all their life, and a concord rich in little things.
They fell together, and of all their prayers this one
Fortune granted, a death joined in the midst of battle.
The twin arms were a glory to the victor Symaethus.

But it was not allowed the Carthaginians to rejoice long
in so great a gift of chance. With menacing terror was at hand
Scipio, pitying the backs of the cohort turned in flight,
and Varro, the source of all the evil, and yellow-haired
Curio and Brutus, descended from the first consul.
And the line, propped by these men, would have repaired the lost
field with a new mass, had not the Carthaginian leader
suddenly with a whirlwind curbed his columns now running forward.
And he, when he saw Varro afar amid the battles
and the lictor flying around him with his red cloak:
'I know the pomp, and I know the insignia.
Such was Flaminius lately,' he said. Then, hot, the keen
anger of his huge shield he foretells with a thunder.
Alas, wretched man! You could have been made equal in death to Paulus,
had it not then, by the gods' anger, been taken from you
to have fallen by Hannibal's hand. How often will you complain,
Varro, to the gods, that you fled the Sidonian sword!
For Scipio, bearing in death a sudden safety with his rapid
charge, †turned upon himself the dangers begun.
Nor does it grieve the Carthaginian, though the honour
of a rich slaughter is snatched away, to have changed his battle
for a greater foe, and at the Ticinus's streams to exact
the penalties for his snatched father, the contest at last offered.
They stood, brought forth on different shores of the world,
such as no other land had seen meet,
equal in Mars and right hand, but in the rest the Latin leader
went before, better in piety and faith.

They leaped down to the troubled battle from a hollow cloud,
Mavors fearing for the son of Scipio, the Tritonian for the Carthaginian,
and at the coming of the gods both battle-lines
trembled, their leaders undaunted. Black, where Pallas turns
her breast, the fire flashes far and wide from the Gorgon's face,
and the aegis twists its hissings with horrid serpents.
Bloody, so that you would believe a twin comet quivered,
gleam her eyes, and on the top of her helmet a generous
crest rolls its waving flames to the stars.
But Mavors, driving the air before with his weapon brandished
and wrapping the field in his shield, wears the breastplate
that pours out Aetnean fires by the gift of the Cyclopes,
and beats the air, rising with his tawny crest.

The leaders, intent on battle, and having measured more closely
how much each in turn would dare, yet perceived
that the arms-bearing gods had come, and, each glad
to be watched by the gods, added wraths to their minds.
And now Pallas with her right hand had twisted aside
the spear, poised with a strong blow from the Carthaginian's breast,
and Gradivus, taught by the example to bring aid
to the fierce goddess, straightway held out the Aetnean
sword to the youth for the battles and bade him greater things.
Then the Virgin, kindling deep within, violent, suddenly
flooded her face with flames, and twisting her sidelong
eyes, surpassed the Gorgon with her troubled visage.
All the monstrous water-snakes raised their huge limbs,
the aegis being shaken, and at the blows of her first frenzy
Mavors himself drew back his foot by degrees from the contest.
Here the goddess, with a swift effort, hurls a torn part
of the neighbouring mountain and rocks bristling with crags
at Mars, raging, and Sason, its shore shaken, took fright
at the sounds carried far back.

But these battles did not deceive the king of the gods.
He quickly sends down Iris, girded with clouds,
to curb the excessive movements, and speaks thus:
'Go, goddess, and swiftly glide to the Oenotrian lands,
and tell my sister to soften her fierce angers
and not to hope to overturn the fixed laws of the Parcae.
Tell her too: ''If you do not desist (for I know the venom and heat
of your flame-bearing mind) and do not gather in your anger,
you shall learn how far the dread thunderbolts excel the aegis.'''
After the Tritonian maiden, hesitating, received this,
nor for long sure enough whether to yield to her father's arms:
'We will withdraw,' she said, 'from the field. But with Pallas driven off,
will he turn aside the fates? And will he keep me from the high heaven
from seeing the fields of Garganus seething with slaughter?'
Having spoken thus, she bore the Carthaginian, lifted in a hollow
cloud, away from the contests, and left the lands.

But fierce Gradivus, at the departure of the goddess returning
to the air, recalls the minds, and those scattered over the plain
he himself with his great hand, wrapped in keen mist,
restores to the battle. The Italians turn their standards and renew,
their fear reversed, a new slaughter.
The keeper set over the winds, whose breaths the prison
holds compressed by his command, and to whom heaven and the rushing
East winds and the North obey, and the West winds and the South,
at the prayers of Juno, who brought no small promises,
unbridles for the battles, on the Aetolian plains, the reigning
Vulturnus. This avenger of her destroying anger pleases her.
He, after he plunged himself into the white pit of Aetna
and conceived fires and brought forth a flaming face,
flies out with a horrendous shriek, and the Daunian realms
he blows through, driving a blind cloud of gathered dust.
The gusts snatched away their eyes and their voice and their hands.
With its sandy white whirl, lamentable to tell,
it whirls balls of it into the faces of the Italians, and rejoices
in the frenzy bidden to war with the companies. Then by the mass of ruin
both soldier and arms and trumpets are laid low on the earth,
and every lance is carried backward, the blast meeting it,
and on the Rutulians the blow falls vainly on their backs.
And the same blast favours the weapons of the Carthaginians,
and, like spears hurled with a throwing-strap, the whirlwind
helps and, shrieking, drives on the Tyrian spears.
Then the soldier, his throat closed with dense dust,
mourns his coward death with his gaping mouth choked.
He himself, his yellow head hidden in the black gloom,
Vulturnus, and his hair drenched with much sand,
now drives those turned from behind with his shrieking wings,
now, coming against their faces in the centre, with the screaming storm
shakes their arms before them and hisses with his open mouth.
At times those intent on battle and now, now on the point of bearing
the steel to the enemy's throat with effort and blow,
he turns aside and tears the right hand from the very wound.
Nor is it enough to befoul the Ausonian cohorts far and wide:
he vomits into the war the air mingled with bellowings,
and twice with his whirlwind he made the topmost crests of the god quiver.

While the Aeolian fury wages these battles against the Roman
squadrons and kindles Mars into wrath,
the Virgin, with Juno as ally, addresses her father:
'How great a flood Gradivus drives into the Punic camp,
look, and with how great slaughters, raging, he fills himself!
Now, I beg, does it not please you that Iris descend to the lands?
Although I came not to destroy the Trojans (since with our pledge
Rome reigns, and I set my seat with the Palladium in this city),
