not to destroy the Trojans, but I refused that the light of her
nursling Libya, Hannibal, be driven from life in his flowering years
and that beginnings so great be extinguished.'
Here Juno takes her up, and from the anger of her long toil:
'Nay,' she said, 'that the nations may know how much the measureless
realms of Jove avail and how much your power, husband,
stands before all the gods, scatter with your blazing
weapon (we ask nothing else) the citadels of Carthage,
and plunge the Sidonian line, in a vast chasm of the earth,
into the Tartarean depths, or overwhelm it with the sea.'
Against this Jupiter answers with gentle face:
'You contend with the fates and stretch out sickly hopes.
He, O daughter, to whom you gladly bore hostile weapons,
that youth shall crush the Tyrians and put on the name of the race
and carry the Libyan laurel to the Capitol.
But he to whom you, wife, give spirit and glory,
(I sing the fates) shall turn his arms away from the Laurentine peoples.
Nor are the bounds of disaster far off. The hour and the day comes
on which he shall wish he had crossed no Alps at all.'
So he says, and quickly sends Iris down from Olympus
to recall Mars and bid him withdraw from the battle.
Nor, having struggled against the prohibition, did Gradivus go off into the high
clouds without a roar, though the war-horns and trumpets
and wounds and blood and shouting and arms gave him joy.

When at last the field lay open, free of the gods' contest,
and loosed of the god, the Carthaginian rushes from the lowest part of the plain,
whither he had gradually fled from the heavenly arms,
drawing with a great voice both horse and men and the mass
of the wild turret-bearing beast and the labours of the engines.
And when he recognized the youth, troubling the troops with his lighter
sword, and his anger sparkled on his bloody
cheeks: 'What Furies or what god,' he said, 'drove you against the foe,
see, Minucius, that you should dare again to entrust yourself to us?
Your father, born of my arms, where is your Fabius now? Once, shameless one,
let it be enough to have escaped our hands.' And then,
the spear, companion to his proud words, with a wall-breaking whirlwind
pierces through his breast and forestalls his coming words with the blow.

Nor is it enough to rage with the iron. The wild beast is brought up
with its black mass, and the Italian manhood is matched against the monsters.
For, riding ahead on his horse, he bids the Moor who guides
the Lucanian oxen into war with his goad to drive on with greater spurs
and to whirl on the herds of the Libyan beasts.
Hugely shrieking it is driven, and, compelled by frequent
wound, the warlike beast bears its hasty steps.
On its livid back sits a tower armed with flame and men
and javelins. From afar the rough hail
of stones falls upon the arms, and far and wide the Libyan, lofty,
pours a flying cloud of weapons from the mound.
A long rampart stands, crowded through the close columns,
with snow-white tusks, and, fixed at close quarters to the ivory, a spear
gleams, its point directed from the curved tip.
Here, amid the alarms of the moment, through limbs, through arms,
the beast drives its wicked tusk into Ufens
and bears him, crying out, carried over the trampled columns.
Nor was Tadius's death lighter: where his breastplate
of many-folded linen closes his side, by degrees the wicked
points of the tusk pierced, his body unhurt,
and bore the man aloft, his shield resounding.
His valour was not shaken off by the terror of the new peril:
he uses the chance for glory, and, near, with his swift sword
pierces through the twin light before its brow.
Goaded by the heavy wound, the beast lifts itself to the air
and, with its legs raised, casts off and hurls the tower far
behind, rolling with its weight bent back.
Arms and men together and the beast, robbed of its sight,
are laid low in a sudden ruin, pitiable, mingled.

Against the fighting monsters the Dardanian leader bids
blazing torches be scattered, and the walls which the beast
carries about to be filled with the sulphur of the black brand.
Nor was there delay at the command. The smoking backs of the elephants
gleam with the gathered flames, and the devouring fire, snatched
by the sounding wind, is borne through the bulwarks.
No otherwise, when a shepherd casts fires on Pindus or Rhodope,
and the burning plague ranges through the woods,
the leafy crags catch fire, and suddenly through the high
ridges the Vulcanian blaze gleams, leaping abroad.
The beast goes, its body glowing with white-hot pitch,
distraught, and parts the squadrons with a wide path.
Nor has anyone valour to take up closer battle:
they dare with far-off javelins and the blow of the reed.
It burns, impatient, and with the heat of its great body
the beast, casting flames hither and thither, kindles them,
until at last it threw itself headlong into the waves
of a neighbouring river, and, deceived by the thin liquid,
through the levels of the standing shoal it bore, driven on,
the flame towering from the long banks. Then at last
it plunged its mass, the deep receiving it, into the gulf.

But where battle is given, and not yet is the Maurusian plague
hot with fire, the Rhoetean manhood, poured around,
now with javelins, now with stones, now with winged lead
assail it from afar, like those who storm fortresses
fortified through high places and besiege citadels.
Daring deeds worthy of the man, worthy of favouring fortune,
the unlucky Mincius had raised his right hand and his sword
close against it in his daring; but the beast, shrieking,
breathing out its panting heat, took away his hand
with its keen coil, entangled in a knot, and twisted it with a dire bond,
and, hurling the wretched man high through the upper air,
dashed him to the earth, lamentable, with his limbs crushed.

Amid these disasters, Varro being seen beneath arms,
Paulus, upbraiding him: 'Why do we not go close,' he said,
'against the Tyrian leader, whom we promised the city
would stand bound, his neck in chains, before your chariot?
Alas, fatherland, alas, commons wicked and crooked in favour!
Never in so hard a lot of evils will you make out
which it should rather have been your prayer never to have been born to you,
Varro or Hannibal.' While Paulus says such things,
the Libyan presses the headlong and against the backs of those rushing
before his eyes rouses all the spears of the leader.
The helmet is beaten and the consul's arms are shaken.
The keener for this, Paulus, fierce, rushes into the midst of the foe.

But then Varro, his mind struck from him, turned, with Paulus
drawn away into trackless contests, and bending his steed
with his hand: 'You pay the penalties, fatherland,' he said,
'who, with Fabius unharmed, called Varro to the wars.
But what discord of mind or of fate
and what hidden trick of the Parcae is there? Long since
it pleases me to break off all things together with the light. But some
god or other holds back my sword. But for what graver things he keeps me!
Shall I live? And shall I carry these broken fasces, scattered
with the blood of my own, back to the people, and shall I give my face
to be gazed on through the angry cities, and—what Hannibal
himself would scarcely demand more savagely—shall I flee and see you, Rome?'
As he protested more, the foes drove him on with closer
weapons, and his steed, the reins loosed, snatched him away.

11. Now come, what peoples and Sarranian camps the famous
disaster on the Iapygian plain turned toward Libya,
I will tell. No faith stands long anywhere for mortals
when Fortune wavers. They strove openly to join their hands
to the Punic, who was breaking the treaties
(alas, too quick to lose faith when affairs are wounded!)—
fiercer than the rest in keeping his wrath stored up
and bold to renew his hatred in time, the Samnite,
and soon, fickle and late to feel shame at the deed,
the Bruttian, and the Apulian, false with his two-faced arms,
then the Hirpinian race, empty and not to be taught repose
and unworthy to have broken faith: as if dire contagions
of a foul disease were spreading through all the peoples.
And now Atella, now Calatia too, drove its cohorts
into the Punic camp, fear overcoming right.
Then the spirited fickleness of Phalantine Tarentum
loosed the Ausonian yoke. Lofty Croton opened
her friendly gates and to barbarous commands
taught the grandsons of the Thespiads to bow their necks to the Africans.
The same madness held Locri too. The shore of the shoaling
strand, where Greater Greece guards her Argive walls
and is washed, curving, by the Ionian deep,
following Libya's glad fortunes and her luck in war,
swore, trembling, its battles to the Tyrian war god.
And now indeed the Celts, the proudest dwellers by the Eridanus,
fell upon the woes of Italy, and old comrades in grief
hastened to join themselves with all their force.

But the Celts might be excused this, and the Boian peoples
their impious wars: that the frenzy which pleased the Senonian race
should please Capua, and that the Dardan walls,
from their first founding, should ally with a barbarian Numidian tyrant—
who now, when the times have so changed, would believe it?
Luxury and the sloth nurtured in mad debauches,
and shame consumed by sinning, and honour, left to wealth alone,
a disgrace—these tore the people gaping
with idleness and the city loosed from its laws.
On top of this, a savage pride drove them to ruin.
Nor was there lack of strength for their vices. To no people
of Ausonia was the measure of gold and silver greater
(so then did Fortune favour them); their cloth was steeped
in Assyrian poison for the men, and in midday
the royal banquets, and feasts caught by the rising sun,
and a life smeared with every stain.
Then the fathers were cruel to the people, the plebs glad
at the senate's hatred, and sedition, striking together
the discordant hearts. But meanwhile a more polluted
old age was enlarging the reckless faults of the youth.
Nor were those whom a base birth and a despised origin
of life disgraced, lacking in hoping for themselves and demanding first
the commands and the reins of the perishing homeland.
Indeed it was an old custom to enliven the banquets of men
with slaughter, and to mingle with the feasts the grim spectacles
of men contending with the sword, and often over the very
cups of the falling, the tables sprinkled with no scant blood.

Approaching these by craft, by which to turn their sick minds
more keenly toward the Tyrians, demanding what he was sure
Rome would by no chance grant (for he did not wish it granted)—
Pacuvius was a name not obscure for its crime—
he urges them to demand a share of the highest power,
and the fasces in turn, with a consul allied,
and, if they should refuse to sit on the divided curule chair,
the honour made equal, and to see the two sets of axes,
that an avenger of the refusal should stand before their eyes and faces.
So a chosen band carries the words at a hurried pace.
Virrius, surpassing all in eloquence, stands foremost,
but of obscure birth, and second to none in frenzy.
When in the gathering of the fathers and the great senate
he had poured out the impious counsels of the mad crowd,
scarcely whole, and inflamed their ears with swelling words,
a harsh clamour bursts from the whole assembly
with the united roar of those who refuse; then each man,
upbraiding, wearies him, and the temple shakes with the strife of voices.

Here Torquatus, noble for having matched his grandfather's
stern brow, said: 'Alas, Capua, bearing such words,
have you hardened yourselves to approach the Romulean walls,
to which Carthage and Hannibal did not dare bring their arms
after Cannae? Does it never pass through your ears,
when on the Tarpeian seat the Latins begged for equality,
how he who then brought the commands with proud mouth
was thrust back—not with words, not with voice, but with a fierce
right hand—driven headlong through the temple's threshold
in so great a whirling of his rolled body,
that, dashed on the cruel rock, with Jove looking on, he atoned
for his grim words and paid for impious speech with death?
Behold, I am the offspring of him who from the seat of the Thunderer
drove out the suppliant and, as consul, defended
the bare Capitol with his hand.' Then, seeing the man rave
and threaten the eyes with the palms of his hands and prepare
to repeat his ancestor's deeds, growing yet harsher in greater stir,
Fabius takes him up, gnashing: 'O wholly shameful!
The seat, behold, is empty, widowed by war's storm:
on whom, I ask, of you do you make ready to set it,
and into Paulus's place whom do you give? Or is your lot,
Virrius, first and before the others, the senate yielding,
and does the purple now summon you and match you with our Bruti?
Go, madman, go where you are heading; let perfidious
Carthage give you her own fasces.' In the midst of the speaker's heat,
unable to hold his fury back longer with a groan,
Marcellus cries out grimly from a lightning wrath:
'What patience, and how slow, holds your mind,
O Varro, too confounded by the war god's whirlwind,
that you can endure, as consul, these frenzied nightmares?
Do you not long since drive them, hurled from the temple's threshold,
headlong to the gates, and force these half-men to learn
what the command of a consul made in our custom is?
A youth never sober and soon to perish, I warn you,
quickly get gone from the city. Before your walls,
as is fitting, the leader, armed, will give the due answer.'
Hereupon all rise alike and press the men with a great clamour.

And too the Campanian youth quickly bore their own step
from the doors, and Virrius, roused by the grief of so great
a rebuff, was turning Hannibal over in his mouth.
Fulvius (for the presages of his mind promised him
the glory to come, and the image of perishing Capua
was even then before his eyes) said: 'Not even if you,
victor, drive to Rome the leader of Carthage bound
in chains at his neck, will it hereafter be granted to enter
the consecrated seats of Quirinus. Make haste, I beg,
where your sick mind calls you.' Then, hurried off, they bear back
these grim answers of the fierce senate, mixed with threats.

Is it your pleasure, almighty one, that the fates lie hidden
sunk in such darkness? A happier age will come one day,
when loyal Rome will rejoice in a Campanian consul
and, secure, will of her own will restore to her great-souled
grandsons the fasces and the arms long denied through wars.
Yet this punishment of their proud forefathers will endure:
that Capua shall not send her men to the voting
before Carthage sends hers. After he had now set forth
the senate's words, now its deeds, then Virrius, mixing false
with true by craft, sang to the troubled the fatal signal
of bloody war. The maddened youth want arms, arms,
and Hannibal. The crowd rushes from every side
and calls the Punic into their homes. The mighty deeds
of the Sidonian youth they celebrate: how he broke the Alps,
the partner of Hercules' glory, and crossed at a run
the crags that neighbour the gods, how, glutted with slaughter,
he closed, victor, the fords of the Eridanus, how the same,
victor, troubled the Lydian pools with Roman blood,
how he gave the banks of the Trebia to the eternal name
of fame, and the same man amid the battles sent both Paulus
and Flaminius, the chief men of the state, down to the shades.
On top of these they heap Saguntum razed in the first war,
and the ridges of the Pyrenees, and the Ebro, and the rites of his father,
and the war sworn by the man in his boyhood years.
That one man, with so many leaders slain in slaughter,
so many routed in the line, stands amid the battles
touched by no weapons. When by the gift of the gods it is granted
to ally one's hands with this man and be joined by treaty,
should Capua, forsooth, endure the pride of a bloodless people
and the empty swelling and the lordship of the city,
which denies the fasces and equal rights as if to slaves?
For truly Varro must be held the worthier of so great a name,
since a consul more resplendent in purple flees him.

Boasting such things, they were already making ready to send
the band chosen by lot, to join the youth by treaty to the Tyrians.
But not the unconquered strength alone within his breast
did Decius then lay aside, the glory of Capua. And he, received
into the midst of the gathering (for it was not granted to delay),
said: 'Citizens, do you go to violate the rights of your fathers
and to join in friendship a head condemned at the altars
of a profaned treaty? What so great forgetting of the right?
It is great, and set among great peoples and men,
to show a faith unturned! Now is the time to enter
battles for the Rutulians, now to move standards and the line,
while affairs are anxious and the wounds demand a cure:
that is the place for duty, when good fortune fails, and when
harsh Fortune calls us to give aid. For to cherish the glad
is in no way the glory of a great spirit. Come here, be present.
I know souls like the gods, and hearts never narrow
in great misfortunes. They take, believe me, Cannae
and the Trasimene shoals and Paulus's memorable death.
These are they who with their hands cast out the foe
fixed in your walls and snatched Capua from the proud
commands of the Samnites. These are they who gave you laws,
terror driven off, and held back the Sidicine wars.
What allies do you flee? Or whom do you add? I am that Dardan
blood, to whom my father left the sacred rites, to whom Capys,
kin to great Iulus, left a name drawn down from Jove;
shall I, that man, among the half-human Nasamones, and among
the savage Garamantian who equals the ways of wild beasts,
pitch my tent, mingled with the Marmaric fosterling,
and follow a leader for whom now, in place of treaty
and justice, there is the sword, and praise drawn from blood alone?
Not so, not so; right and wrong are not so mingled for Decius
that he could wish for this. With no such great gift has grudging
Nature armed us as that the door of death
lies open and the power to leave a life that is unjust.'

These vain words Decius hurled to turned-away ears.
But the chosen band was making the treaty with the Punic.
And now there was at hand, sent ahead to the leader amid the troubling
tumult, a numerous cohort of Autololes. He himself with a great column
swiftly moved his hastened standards across the plains.
And Decius: 'Now is the hour, men, now the time. Be present,
while a right hand worthy of Capua, with me as leader,
attempts the avenging deed: let the barbarous host fall down.
Each for himself, eager, seize this glory. If the foe
prepares to approach, offer him gates blocked with corpses
and purge the wickedness with the sword. This blood alone,
in the end, shall wash the minds stained with the crime.'

And while he proclaims these things in vain, pleasing to none,
the harshness of the man and his fierce undertaking being heard,
bearing a heart big with much wrath, the Punic
was standing at the walls and bids the chosen quickly fetch
relentless Decius to the camp. His bristling valour
and a breast armed with good faith and the desire of the right
and a mind greater than Capua, undaunted by the great peril,
stood unconquered, and with grim face assailed
the leader's menacing commands with bitter words besides.
Him the ruler of Libya, scorning the bearer of so many standards,
so many arms, upbraiding, with a great clamour proclaims:
'After Paulus, after Flaminius, am I matched, alas,
with mad Decius, who wished to contend with me
for the honour and fame of death. Seize (go, hurry)
the standards, leaders. Whether the Campanian city
lies open to me against Decius's will, I am pleased to learn—
to me, who, stirring new wars, found the Alps lying open,
rocks thrusting at the sky and trodden by one god alone.'
Blood had suffused his face, and from his grim eye
flames rose. Then his foaming mouth and the sighs driven
from his panting throat rolled a dire murmur deep within.
So, borne into the city, the whole senate accompanying him
and the crowd alike rushing to gaze on the leader's face,
he pours out all his rage and the storms of his wrath.

And too, nearer perils had inflamed Decius's mind,
and he saw the time was now at hand
when, unarmed, he might surpass the praises of the unconquered leader.
No flight, no shut house hid him,
but free, as if no Hannibal had entered the city,
he had kept his leisure with undaunted face,
when, dreadful, a band roused with savage arms
attacks the youth and sets him at the feet of the leader,
seated on high. Then from above, assailing him with fierce words,
the victor thunders: 'Do you alone make ready to prop up
rushing Rome and call her back from her death,
O madman? Behold, the man who would snatch from me
the great gifts of the gods. For Decius, forsooth, an idle one,
was I kept, to be conquered—by unwarlike Decius, to whom no woman
born on the Agenorean shores of our Carthage
would yield. To this man, come (for why should we, great-souled,
bear unworthy things?), soldier, fasten the chains he has earned.'
He had said these things, and the taunts knew no end yet:
as when a lion, borne among the herds, sets himself
upon the high necks, and victorious roars monstrously
in his wrath, and, heavy, clings with sunk claws,
hanging on the neck, gnaws the panting bullock.
But Decius, while they bind the chains, says: 'Fasten quickly
(for so it befits Hannibal to have entered) the chains,
the price of the ill-omened treaty. So a victim fully
worthy falls, Decius. For it is not right that you, glad
in human blood, should have appeased it by slaying bullocks.
See, your hand! See, your treaty! Not yet has the senate-house,
not yet the posts of the temples been entered by you: already
by a fierce command the prison is opened. Go on, and to such
beginnings heap deeds to match. Fame will bear to the shades
that you were crushed, fallen in the ruins of Capua.'
Nor was he allowed to speak more. His head is veiled
in black cloth, and, fierce, he is dragged before the faces of his own.

Then the victor, exulting, his breast calmed at last,
glad to look on the city's buildings and temples,
carries his serene eyes around and learns each thing:
who founded the walls, and how great the youth under arms,
how many talents of silver and bronze lie open for war,
now what manner of mounted force, now in turn how great
the foot-soldiers' force of men. They show the lofty Capitol
and tell of the Stellate plains and bountiful Ceres.
And now Phoebus with his wearied horses was driving the day
to its goal in Olympus, and Hesperus was darkening
with shadow gradually poured the chariot hastening to the shores:
they set out the banquet in their custom and through the festal city
celebrate feasts at tables royally heaped.
He himself, deemed worthy of a god's worship and sacred honour,
is received on high upon couches of choice and far-shining purple.
Not one throng of servants: to some was given the care
of laying out the food, to some to tend the hearths,
to some to bear the cups in order;
and too the larder is built up at fixed places. On the rough table
gleam the weights of gold engraved from of old.
The flames steal away the night, and with the din of those who move
the lofty house murmurs. The Sidonian soldier, unused
to the rich table, marvels, and drinks in with wondering eyes
the unknown face of proud luxury.
He himself eats in silence and condemns such honours
to be given to feasts, and that tables should be so easily served
by so great a column, until hunger was driven off and the gifts
of Bacchus loosed his hard mind. Then at last
the gladness was given back to his brow, and the heavier cares
laid down from his breast.

Teuthras resounds with his Euboean lyre, a dweller
of Cumae, and soothes with songs the ears deafened by the harsh
murmur of the savage war-trumpet amid battles.
For he sang of Chaos, once a blind mass without a star,
no day arising, and a world without light.
Then how the god had parted the pools of the liquid deep
and set the globe of earth in the midst of the frame;
how he had given the lofty Olympus for the gods to dwell on,
and he showed the chaste ages of father Saturn.
And now he sang of Jove and his glad loves through stealth,
and the bridals of Electra, daughter of Atlas, whence was born
Dardanus, an offspring worthy of the gods, and how he gave
to the Thunderer Erichthonius, a grandson of great stock;
hence Tros, hence Ilus, then in the long order of the race
Assarcus, and how Capys, less than none in fame or hand,
gave his name to the first walls.
Together with applause the Sidonian youth alike
and the Campanian bands celebrate it. Before all the leader
pours libation from the goblets to the honour of the name
with august rite; the rest, who follow him,
in Bacchus's manner sprinkle the liquor on the tables
and the throng grows hot with wine.

Meanwhile, when the Tyrian gathering had dissolved into joys
(for I will not, youth not unworthy of being silenced,
gladly pass over your beginnings and deny you fame,
though your daring, though of great promise, was unfulfilled),
one mind, untouched by wine and disarmed by no poisons
of drinking from its honour, was rolling in its silent breast
the mass of Sidonian battle and slaughter.
And, that so sacred a longing might be the more to be marvelled at,
born of Pacuvius, he had condemned his father's arts.
He, following close behind his father, who, laden with various
banquets, was leaving the halls with slow step,
after it was given him to disclose his plans and unfold
his new attempts, and a free place, the rest of the buildings
left behind, lay open at their backs, said: 'Receive
counsels worthy of both Capua and us': (and, his toga
drawn aside, he bares his armed side) 'this war
I make ready to finish with this sword and to bear off, torn,
to the Thunderer the head of the Libyan ruler, victorious. This will be
that sword which will now seal the treaties polluted by guile.
If old age cannot bear so great a spectacle
and trembles, weary with years, at deeds too great,
then do you withdraw to a safe house and leave me
to my own purpose. He whom you believe the highest and match
with the gods, Hannibal—O how much greater in name
than the Punic will your son now be to you!' From his face
flashed a fierce fire, and the man's spirit was already waging the war,
when the old man, scarcely now able with sick ear long since
to bear the weight of so great an attempt, trembling there
sinks down and, fixing frequent fearful kisses on his feet:
'By whatever of life remains, by a father's rights,
and by your safety, dearer to me, son, than my own,
desist from your enterprise, I beg, lest I see
hospitality polluted with blood, and cups filled
with bloody gore, and the tables overturned in the strife of battle.
Will you—he whom not battle-lines, not walls and cities
can withstand, when his nearer brow and eye flash
with quivering fire—will you endure those thunderbolts
that the man pours from his head, if, at the sight of the sword,
he hurls the dire voice with which he turns the columns across the plains?
It deceives you, that you think him unarmed among the tables.
A majesty eternal, sought by the man in so many wars,
won by so many slaughters, arms the leader. If you bring your face near,
you will marvel that Cannae and the Trebia, before your eyes,
and the Trasimene graves, and the mighty shade of Paulus stand there.
What then? In so great a crisis, will the hands of his companions
lying near him grow numb? Spare him, I beg, and cease to wish
for one whom, victor, you could not survive. Or do the grim chains
and Decius not teach you to compose your mind?'

Recounting such things, when he saw the youth blazing
with love of greater fame and deaf to fear,
he said: 'I ask nothing more; carry your step back to the feast;
let us make haste: no longer must you pierce with your hand
the breasts of the Sidonian youth that guard the king:
test your right hand on this throat. For here is your steel,
if you make ready to attack the Punic—through these vitals
of mine the steel must be drawn. Do not scorn slow old age.
I will set my limbs against you, and the sword denied you
to wrench away I will snatch by my death.' Then tears poured
from his face, and the Punic, by the great care of the gods,
was preserved for the arms of Scipio's son, nor did the fates
grant that so great a deed be wrought by a foreign hand. Most fair
in his wrath, and worthy to have become master of his memorable
venture, how great a praise he lost when the attempt was laid down,
for whom merely to have wished so great a thing is glory. Then they hasten
to give themselves back to the feast and clear the grimness from their brows,
until sleep dissolved the glad banqueting of the men.

The next light was making ready to bring forth Phaethon's horses,
its chariot now gleaming swift beneath the topmost waves,
and the youth begotten of great Hamilcar long since
plies his hard cares. Mago, fierce, is bidden to go
to the citadels of Carthage and bear to the fathers
news of the leader's deeds. Plunder and captive bodies
are gathered, and the spoils stripped from the men in bloody war,
the offerings of a war made prosperous by the gods.
Another of his cares is dismissed from the Libyan shores—
alas, Decius, kept for the leader's slow wrath on his return,
had not Jupiter, pitying the youth's undeserved punishment, from on high
turned him toward the ancient city of Battus.
Here men bearing the Pellaean sceptres of Ptolemy
snatched him from his threats, and the bonds were loosed from his neck.
And the same earth, guardian of his life, soon afterward
received his unviolated bones in a quiet tomb.

Nor meanwhile did the longed-for time escape Venus,
to crush the minds of the Punic through prosperity with blind
ruin, and to tame their restless hearts with luxury.
She bids her sons scatter their deceiving darts on every side
with their hands and send the silent flames into their breasts.
Then, smiling sweetly on the boys: 'Let proud Juno go
and despise us (no wonder, for what are we?), boasting of her
deeds with the favourable. She is strong in her hand, strong in her arms:
we, with a boyish bow, slowly pour our little
darts, and there is no blood from our wound.
But come, O my throng, I pray (now is the time), be present
and burn up the Tyrian youth with your silent weapons.
By embrace and much wine and the sleep of men
must that battle-line be overthrown which the sword has not broken,
nor fires, nor the war god with reins let loose.
Let the leader drink in the luxury that has glided through his vitals,
nor let it shame him to have lain propped on a painted couch,
nor let him strive against drenching his hair with Assyrian balm.
Let that boaster, who would draw out his sleep under the wintry sky,
rather choose to spend his nights indoors,
and let him lay aside the custom of eating while he sits
often on his galloping horse beneath his helmet, and let him learn
to give the unwarlike day to wine. Then, dripping
after the feasts, let the lyre be welcome, and let him slothful pass
the slumbrous nights, or his wakeful ones, beneath our power.'
When Venus had said this, the wanton army of cupids
applauds and lets itself down from high heaven on snowy wings.
The Moorish youth feels the flame-bearing pinions,
and alike their breasts grew warm with the scattered darts.
They want the gifts of Bacchus and feasts and songs again,
melted by the Pierian lyre. No keen war-horse sweats
in the open field, no whirled lance through the air
exercises their bared arms.
Waters softened by flames warm their limbs languishing
in sleep, and by wretched goods their bristling valour perishes.
The leader himself too, breathed upon by deceiving Cupid,
renews the tables with banquets and seeks again
the hospitality of the willing, and gradually, faded,
puts off his native arts, the hidden arrow corrupting his mind.
Now Capua is called a second homeland and, under equal
honour, a second Carthage, and the vices that allure
shake the genius untouched by second fortune.
Nor is there any limit to the luxury and to the life sunk
in lust among the Campanians: they heap it up and through various
arts of the stage strive to mark out their feasts with shows,
as wanton Memphis with its Amyclaean Canopus
constantly resounds the Phrygian lotus-pipe to Nilotic strains. †
Above all, sweetly, while the Punic rejoices, through their ears
now Teuthras pours the song with his voice, now with his plectrum.
And he, when he saw the leader of Libya marvelling
at the strings sounding under his thumb, beginning then gently
to sing the proud praises of the Aonian lyre,
moved through his songs a tongue harmonious with the cithara,
such as could surpass the swans that leave their life,
and chose from many these gentlest themes for the table:
'For the Argive peoples once, wondrous to tell,
a lyre was heard, blest, with its tortoise-shell to draw
the stone and to set the willing rocks upon the walls.
This walled Thebes with Amphion's plectrum,
and, the flint summoned to the ramparts climbing of itself,
bade the sung towers rise into the immense.
Another, ruling the troubled deep with its quill,
both held the seals and drew Proteus in every shape
and bore Arion on its watery back.
Now the lyre, beloved of the Centaur, that on the Pelian crag
shaped by song the minds of heroes and the heart of great
Achilles, could check the wraths, struck on its string,
of either the sea or grim Avernus.
But the strings that Orpheus struck by the Riphaean Strymon,
heard by the gods above, heard by the shades,
shine bright among the stars in a heaven well-earned.
Him too his mother, with all the throng of his sisters,
the Aonides, accompanying, his mother marvelled at as he sang.
Not while he sang did the Pangaean ridges or Mavortian Haemus
stand, not at his music the farthest Thrace:
the wild beasts came with the woods, the rivers with the mountains,
and the bird, forgetful of its sweet nest and its flight laid by,
unmoved, hung captive in the air.
Indeed, when the Pagasaean ship, the blue waters not yet
known, terrified them and forbade them to enter the deep,
. . .
the sea, drawn by the song, came to the stern
of the sacred keel, the cithara enticing it. The pale realms
the Bistonian bard and Acheron, sounding with flames,
he appeased with his quill, and fixed the rolling stone.
O dire Ciconian mothers and Getic frenzies
and Rhodope condemned by the gods! Hebrus bore his torn-off face
into the sea, both banks following it.
Then too, when the swift waves bore the head cut from the neck,
suddenly there flashed through the waves
the sea-beasts, leaping over the whole deep at the murmur.'

So then Pierian Teuthras with his Castalian song
was breaking the men's breasts, hardened by wars.
Meanwhile gentle breezes had now brought Mago
to the Libyan lands. Wreathed with laurel the ship was entering
the longed-for harbour, and over the sea gleamed
captive arms from afar, shining on the lofty prow.
But rising long since from the broad water, far and wide
the sailors' shout filled the resounding shores,
and at once, the oars striking against the drawn-back breasts,
the sea broke and foamed with a hundredfold lashing.
Nor slow does the crowd run out into the midst of the waves
to seize the joy, and the throng, lifted up by favour,
celebrates in rivalry the new joys with vast applause.
The leader is made equal to the gods: him on every side the mothers,
him the lesser throng of grandsons, warned to rejoice,
and the band of elders, and nearby both people and fathers,
deign with the honour of the gods, with bullocks slain.
So Mago entered his homeland and the gates exulting
with the fame of his brother's praise. Then the senate rushes forth,
and the senate-house is thronged with a great gathering of the fathers.
Then, having worshipped the gods of his grandsire in the ancient custom,
he says: 'I announce a glorious war and the broken
resources on which the Italian land relied—I myself
no small part of the toils. We fought, the gods favouring our prayers.
There is a place that the glory of an Aetolian king marks out,
possessed once among the ancient ages by Daunus.
The Aufidus surrounds the moist fields with rapid eddy
and cuts off the lands with its overflowing pools,
soon strikes the Adriatic waves and with great roar
drives the yielding sea back into the deep.
Here Varro and Paulus, a great name among the Latin names,
to whom, as leaders of the state, power was entrusted,
the gloom of dark night scarce yet driven off,
invade the plain, and with their arms gleaming far and wide
of their own accord kindle the light of the rising East.
We against them (for keen frenzy drove my brother
to the longed-for fight) move the swift standards from the camp.
Both the earth trembles, and stricken Olympus bellows.
Here the leader hid the river and the plains with the slaughter
of men, than whom never did the lands bring a greater
commander to wars. I saw, when with savage whirlwind
and din Ausonia, routed through the bellowing fields,
gave its back to one man. I saw when Varro was carried off
on his galloping horse, degenerate, his arms cast aside.
Indeed I saw you too, great-souled Paulus, your body pierced
with weapons, falling over the slaughter of your comrades.
That day avenged Aegates and the lavish servile treaties
by slaughter: it would have pleased to wish for no more
than the kindly god then granted. If a second light
like that should return, you would be the one chief
of all peoples then, Carthage, and be worshipped through all lands.
These are witnesses of the slaughter, which the proud men
are wont to bear on the left as an illustrious sign.' Then is poured
before the faces of those who marvel a ring far-flashing with gold,
and gives faith to his words, notable for no small heap.
Hence, taking up again, 'It remains now,' he says, 'that Rome,
already undermined, be turned from her deepest foundations
and levelled with the ground. Let us strive: restore the strength
drained by so many misfortunes, and let the treasuries lie open,
not sparingly, to the hands that we have bought with war.
The beast already fails us, the grim terror of the Ausonians,
and too the provisions wear out.'

And while he tells these things, turning his face with grim
look upon Hanno, whom his swelling glory had long since
goaded, crooked man, with bitter envy of the leader's zeal:
'Do we now prove our hands and our enterprises to you?
Is it now right that I not serve the Dardan colonist?
Or does it please you to surrender Hannibal a second time?
You whose breast wells black with the poison of envy
and with black gall, won over at last by so many titles,
by so many trophies, unhappy man, be silent. Behold the hand,
behold the right hand, which you would have given to the Aeneadae
to mangle—it has filled both shores and rivers
and pools and the broad plains with blood.'
So Mago, and no obscure favour fed his spirits.
To him, with both envy and wrath goading, Hanno:
'Such taunts of a mad youth I marvel at
not at all: he swells with his nature, and you would not be slow
to recognize the brotherly heart and the empty venom of his tongue.
That he may not believe me changed, ceasing for empty things,
I am the author that now we must beg for peace, now, the treaty
broken, lay down our wicked arms and beware the deadly war.
And indeed weigh for yourselves, I beg,
what he brings: no other course is left for us to judge.
He begs for weapons, men, gold, fleets, provisions,
and a war-beast. Conquered, I would have given no more.
We have glutted the Rutulian fields with Dardan blood,
and Latium lies in the plains. To lay aside our cares
at last therefore, good man, grant as victor, and let it be allowed to sit
in our homeland, allowed not to drain our households,
often emptied, with the costs of rapacious war.
Now, behold, now, I say (let my presages be false,
I pray, and my mind be mocked by an empty augury),
the deadly day is not far off. I know his savage
heart and foresee the wraths born of disasters.
You, I fear you, you, Cannae. Lower your standards
and even try, come now, and demand peace:
it will not be given. That grief, believe me, prepares a greater
ruin from his loss, and these treaties the victor
will grant sooner than the conquered. And indeed, you who sound
such great deeds with proud mouth and blow with a foaming whirlwind
on the ears of the ignorant, tell me, lo, that brother of yours
in arms, equal to the war god, whom the earth through the ages
never bore a leader like for the wars,
why has he not yet seen the walls of the Romulean city?
Are we, forsooth, to snatch from their mothers' bosom into the foe
those not yet fit to carry heavier arms,
are we bidden to weave a thousand bronze-bound keels,
and is a war-beast to be sought through all the lands of Libya,
that Hannibal may prolong his long commands and the armed years,
and drag out his rule even into the times of fate?
But you (for we are not surrounded by hidden craft),
do not despoil your sweet homes, and set a measure
to the camps and wealth of the powerful. Peace, the best of things
that it is given to man to know, peace alone better than triumphs
beyond number, peace able to guard our safety
and make the citizen equal—let it be called back at last
to the Sidonian citadels, and let the fame, Phoenician,
of your perfidy be driven from the city. If so great a lust
for arms holds him and he persists in not yielding the swords
to the homeland that demands them, I urge that nothing
be supplied to his frenzy, and that Mago carry these words to his brother.'

As he was knitting on more (for he had not glutted his wrath
by speaking), the clamour of those who willed otherwise troubles him:
'If the glory of Libya, surpassable by no man's arms,
Hannibal, is your wrath, shall we abandon the victor
at the very goal and not bring aids of wealth,
that the envy of one man may hold back the sceptres now all but won?'
Then, eager, they grant what the use of war demanded
and boast their favour, the man absent, before this witness.
Soon it was resolved to carry the same to the Spanish lands,
while base malice disparages immortal deeds
and does not let the leader's praises grow by their aid.

12. Now harsh Winter was hiding her icy head, her temples
teeming with rains, and her cloudy brow with its south-bearing crest,
and gentle Spring with caressing Zephyrs soothed
the healthful fields with mild, clear weather.
The Punic bursts forth from Capua and shakes the neighbouring lands
far and wide with terror sent ahead, as, hidden through the winter
while the Riphaean blasts of the north wind freeze,
a serpent at last uncoils its limbs from its secret den,
and, the day promising warmth, flashes forth renewed and bears
its glittering head and breathes out venom from its lifted jaws.
But when the standards of the Libyan leader gleamed across the fields,
all was deserted in fear, and, dread persuading,
they shut themselves at once within their rampart, and, anxious for safety,
trembling, awaited the foe at their very walls.

But that vigour was not now in him which, the Alps broken through,
had borne arms in and opened roads, and, master of the Trebia,
had defiled the Maeonian waves with Italian blood.
Soaked with soft luxury and wine,
his limbs flowed slack, torpid † by the allurements of sleep.
He who was wont to drag out the icy nights, weighed down
in his breastplate beneath an unfriendly sky, and often
to scorn his tent when the winter clouds rushed down with hail,
and not even by night were his shields or swords laid aside,
nor his quivers or javelins, and his arms served him for limbs—
now the helmet seemed a heavy burden, and the weights
of the bucklers greater, and the spears poured down with no whirring.

Gentle Parthenope first felt him renewing the contests,
not rich in resources, not despised for valour,
but the harbours drew the leader, willing it, and the safe
waters that the ship coming from Carthage might seek.
One of the Sirens gave her own name (memorable thing)
to the walls, Parthenope, daughter of Achelous, over whose sea
the songs reigned long, when through the waves she sang
a sweet destruction, no boon to the wretched sailors.
Now there are gentle ways for the city, and leisure
hospitable to the Muses, and an age exempt from heavier cares.
Attacking these walls from behind (for the sea had closed the front),
the Punic was not able to break through any roads
with his whole force, and in vain, inglorious in his venture,
he battered the blocked gates, shaking them with the ram.
The victor stood before the Greek defences of Cumae
in vain, and proved the counsels of his cautious mind
by the event, who, after the watery realm of Daunus,
through blood had abstained from going to the Tarpeian citadels.
'Behold, you who have boasted that we are slow and know not
to add speed to our deeds, because of late it was not granted you
to scale the walls of Rome from the battle-line itself—
enter, and the feast promised on the Thunderer's seat
render to these houses, which a Greek hand defends.'
Such things he boasted, and, through shame of fame to come
if, balked of his enterprise, he should retreat from the first city,
he dared all and sharpened his swords with stratagems.
But sudden flames flowed over the walls, and through all
the rampart's winding the unforeseen weapons flew through the air.
Just as, when the tawny bird of Jove has hidden its young
on a rock's height, if with silent effort a serpent
has climbed to the summit and frightens it, close, with its gaping mouth,
she, assailing the foe with her beak and the claws accustomed
to bear the thunderbolts, flies round the circuit of her nest.

At last, wearied, he turned to the neighbouring harbours of Cumae
and set himself to provoke fortune with varied movement
and to stand against his sinister fame by stirring trouble.
But Gracchus, guardian of the city, a defence more sure
than the very walls, kept him off and forbade him again
to sit before the gates and again to hope for entrance.
Helpless in spirit, he ranges and searches all about,
borne on his winged horse, and again begins to drive his men
with exhortations of glory: 'By the gods,' he says, 'what limit
is there to standing before Greek cities, soldier forgetful
of your own deeds? What measure will there be? Before the Alps
stands, no doubt, a greater mass, and I bid you scale the heaven,
battering its crags. Yet, were a second land like that one given,
and other cliffs to rise suddenly beneath the stars,
will you not go, and bear arms aloft with me leading?
Does, alas, the gaping mound of Cumae and its wall
still hold you, or Gracchus, who has not dared to be moved
from his gates? In a small crisis I see
. . .
or shall the nations, whatever you have won by toil,
think your deeds done by chance? By you, the Tyrrhene
pools of the favouring gods, by the Trebia and the ashes of Saguntum
I entreat, render yourselves now worthy of your own fame,
which you trail, and call Cannae back into your hearts.'

So the leader strove to rouse the minds worn by luxury
and frayed by prosperity, and to stay them with words.
And here, surveying the approaches, he sees the gleaming
temples of the citadel on the ridge, whose first beginnings
Virrius then, the relentless leader of lofty Capua, unfolds.
'This which you look upon,' he says, 'is not of our age:
greater hands made it. When (so the tale is) Daedalus
feared to leave the lands and the realm of the Dictaean king,
he found out a way to give no track to one following
over the whole world, daring to raise himself into the airs
of heaven on an alien wing and to show man flight.
Here, balancing his hanging body in the midst of the clouds,
he swam through them and, a new bird, frightened the gods above.
He taught his son too, beneath the likeness of false plumage,
to attempt the ways of birds, and, fallen with the oars
of his pinions loosed and his unhappy wings,
he saw him beating the troubled straits. And while he gives way
to grief, his palms beaten suddenly against his breast,
unwitting, alas, he guided his flight with that mourning movement.
Here, grateful, in place of his cloud-wandering passage, he founded
the holy temple of Phoebus and laid aside his daring wings.'

So Virrius: but the leader counted the idle days
passed without war, and was ashamed to stand still.
He groans at his reverses, and, looking back at the houses he could not take,
makes ready to glut his grief on the city of Dicarchus.
Here too now the sea, now the stony mass of the wall
hinders his daring and the labours of the defenders.
And while a slow toil holds his comrades, striving to break through
the hard and barred ways, he himself surveys the wonders
of the pools and of the land nearby together.

The chief men of Capua are present: he teaches them whence
the warm Baiae take their name, and shows that the pools
gave their own names to a companion of the Dulichian ship.
But this man records that the names of Cocytus once
remained at the Lucrine, and in the midst of the eddy of the sea
commends the Herculean path, where the son of Amphitryon,
victor over the Iberian herd, split the water.
That man shows Avernus, once called Styx by the peoples,
its name changed, now mild and famed among the pools:
then, bristling with a grim grove and blackening shadows,
and feared, it vomited a deadly venom into the sky,
poured forth, lethal to birds, and, sacred through the cities
by Stygian awe, kept its savage honour.
A marsh near to it (the tale is that it opens a way
to the waves of Acheron) loosens its dark jaws
with a standing whirlpool and opens dreadful chasms of the earth,
and at times troubles the shades with new light.
But hard by, they tell, the Cimmerian homes lay,
dim and through the long age pressed by infernal mists
beneath a pallid shadow, and the deep night of the Tartarean city.
Then they point out the fields ever panting with sulphur
and fire and seething bitumen. The earth, the black vapour
welling up, sighing and warmed long with its burnt marrow,
boils and breathes Stygian blasts into the air;
it labours and hisses fearfully from its trembling caverns, †
and at times, struggling to break its hollow seats
or to escape by the straits, with a menacing sound Mulciber
bellows mournfully and gnaws the torn vitals of the earth
and shakes the eaten-out mountains with his murmur.
They tell that the Giants, laid low by Hercules' mass,
shake the earth thrown upon them, and that with their panting breath
the fields are scorched far and wide, and that, whenever they threaten
to break the frame set upon them, the sky grows pale.
Prochyta appears, allotted savage Mimas,
Inarime appears far off, which with its black whirlwind
presses smoking Iapetus, as he hurls flames from his rebel
mouth and, if ever it be granted him to escape,
wishes to renew his wars against Jove and the gods above.
The ridges of Vesuvius are shown, and on the topmost peak
the crags fed upon by flames, and the mountain laid low in ruin
all around, and rocks contending with the fate of Etna.
And too he sees Misenus, keeping the Idaean name in his tomb,
and Herculean Bauli on the very shore:
he marvels at the menaces of the sea and the labours of the land.

When these had been surveyed by the man, returning thence
to the lofty walls of the son of Pheres, he lays waste
the leafy summits of Gaurus, glad with the joyous vine.
Hence he swiftly moves his columns to Chalcidian Nola.
Nola sits on the plain, ringed about in a circle with frequent
towers, and guards with its rampart the level easy to approach;
but Marcellus brought help and aid—one who would give
the arms to be defended not to the towers, but would of his own will
protect the walls with his right hand.
And he, when from afar he sees the Agenorean approach across the plain
and a cloud borne toward the walls, cries: 'Arms, the bloody
foe is here, take up your arms, men,' and he takes them up.
The swift young men stand round and fit to his roaring helm
the bloody crests in their custom. Then he resounds, disposing
the columns at a quick step: 'You shall keep the threshold
of the right gate, Nero; you, turn your cohorts to the left,
Tullus, the bright glory of the Volsci, with the ancestral
standards of Larinum. But when bidden,
through the silence, with a sudden force burst the gates
and pour a storm of weapons onto the plains. I myself will be borne,
the gate torn open, into the midst, and draw the cavalry's combats.'

And while Marcellus does this, already the Punic
were trying to wrench off the bars and, scorning ladders,
to break through the walls. Trumpets sounded everywhere,
and the shout of men and the neighing, with the clarions
and, in the hoarse tumult, the horns, and the arms shaken
on their raging limbs. The bitter plague is borne,
quickened, the gates flung apart, and the squadrons rush out,
poured forth in an unforeseen flood,
as a wicked river overflows, its dams broken,
as the sea, driven by the north wind, is dashed against the rocks,
as the winds, their prison broken, invade the lands.
Nor at the sight of the torrent of arms and men can the Libyan
stand, cast down from hope. The Dardan leader presses
the astonished one, his horse going before, and, leaning his spear
on the backs of those who rush, now wearies his comrades with his voice:
'Go on, come, bear forward your steps. The god is kind, the hour is ours.
This is the way to the walls of Capua,' now again, turned
against the foe: 'Stand. Where are you swept off? Not at the backs
of your men, but at you, leader of Libya, do I cry: stand.
The plain and arms and Mars are in our hands. I dismiss
the cohorts from the slaughter: let us be seen alone.
Marcellus, I demand battle.' So the Latin ruler,
and the honour of attacking the Barcaean youth in fight,
and the prize of the peril, urged him on.

But Juno did not behold these things with a calm breast,
and turned him from his enterprise as he rushed to his final fate.
He labours to stay the routed and recall them:
'Do we come out such as this from the bosom of Capua
and her sinister houses? Stand, O wretches, to whom the highest
glory is a disgrace. Nothing today, believe me, faithful
awaits you turning your backs. You have deserved
that all Ausonia rush upon you, and by savage war you have made it
that no hope of peace or life should remain for the routed.'
He overcame the trumpets with his clamour, and by the force
of his voice, savage, penetrated the ears though they were stopped.

In the arms of Polydamas the young Pedianus
waged war, fierce, and boasted of his Trojan seed and lineage
and of himself from the Antenorid stock,
of no lighter fame in his line, and his glory by sacred Timavus
and a name beloved on the Euganean shores.
To him father Eridanus and the Venetian peoples in order
and the folk rejoicing in Aponus, whether he stirred wars
or, peaceful, preferred the Muses and the silence
of a learned life and to soothe his toils with the Aonian quill,
called none his equal, nor was another youth more known
to the war god, nor another more known to Phoebus.
He, when, pressing the tracks of the Punic with loosened
reins, near him recognized the helmet and the emblem,
the spoil of slain Paulus (a boy bore those,
glad in the leader's no small gift, Cinyps,
Cinyps beloved by the Punic, than whose face
none was more pleasing, and on no brow shone more of grace:
such as the ivory that the air of Tibur feeds, flashing
and ever new, or as the stone that with a wondrous honour
of whiteness shines in the ear, brought from the Red waves)—
when Pedianus saw him, notable for his crests and his known
helmet, gleaming at the rear of the column,
as if a sudden image of Paulus had risen before his eyes
from the infernal seats and demanded back his lost arms,
he attacks, gnashing: 'Will you, most cowardly, bear
the coverings of a sacred head, which not without crime
and the gods' envy your leader would wear?
Behold Paulus.' Then he calls the man to the spectacle of the shades
and drives a piercing weapon into the fleeing one's ribs.
Then, sliding from his horse, with his right hand he tears off
the helmet and the emblems of the great consul and despoils the gleaming youth.
All his beauty is loosed by death, and through his snowy limbs
goes the Stygian colour and ravages the honours of his form.
His ambrosial locks fell, and his violated neck,
the throat sinking, sank back upon his marble shoulder.
Just as the Cytherean fire, returning over Ocean,
when it boasts itself to Venus with its splendour restored,
if a sudden cloud invades it, is dimmed and, waning
in the black darkness, hides its languishing light.
Pedianus himself too, the helmet snatched, astonished
stands stunned at the bare face and checks his wrath.
Then, bearing back the helmet with a great shout to his comrades,
he shook his fierce horse, that bloodied with savage bite
the foaming reins. To him Marcellus, turbulent in arms,
bore his face to meet him in swift tumult,
and recognizing the glory: 'Bravo, O of ancestral valour,
bravo, son of Antenor! Now,' he said, 'let us seek
the snatched coverings of the Libyan leader, what remains,'
and, blazing, with dreadful whirrings he hurls the savage spear.
Nor perhaps would he have been baulked of his vow, had not the opposing
force of Gestar held the weapon with his interposed body.
He, while he protects the leader with arms close by,
the heavy spear, thirsting not for his blood, passed through him
and, his death changed, fulfilled its mighty threats.
The leader is carried off in haste from the crisis of death,
troubled, and, raging, takes his course toward the camp.

And now the army of the Punic, immoderate in flight,
stretches its headlong step in a contest, their arms turned about.
The foe overtakes them with weapons, and one by one
glut their long wraths from the disasters, and to the sky
in rivalry display their swords bloody, and to the avenging gods.
That day first taught what no one would dare
believe of the gods, that the leader of Libya could be checked
in the contest of war. They drag off chariots and men
and the Massylian beast, and bear back coverings torn
from the living warriors, and depart, content to have seen
the leader's back beneath their spear. Then they match Marcellus
in war's glory: he walks with triumph attending,
greater than if as victor he bore the spoils to the Thunderer.

Then raging, after he scarcely drove the foe from his rampart,
the Agenorean leader: 'When have I washed this stain
and with how much enemy blood? Has Ausonia chanced
to see my back? Do you, highest of the gods,' he says,
'after the Trebia judge me worthy of so foul a death?
And you, youth long unconquered, now, alas, without war,
worn down by the goods of Capua—I myself, not degenerate
of my deeds, have turned my victorious standards from the Ausonians:
to you I gave my back. I saw, when I called you to the wars,
you flee no otherwise than from an Italian leader, terrified.
What is left to you of your old war-spirit, you who can give your backs
while I call you back?' Such things the Punic poured forth.
But the Latin squadrons, bearing their spoils,
bore themselves toward the walls of Nola with notable clamour.

But Rome, grievously accustomed for long to hear of the fortunes
of her own, and never restored by prosperity,
when at last news of a favourable battle was brought,
is lifted up and rises by this first gift of the gods.
Before all, the youth, sluggish for war and fleeing toils,
while the war thundered, and who stole themselves away,
pay the penalty of their hiding. Then those who, by the sweetness
of life, found out wiles and corrupted the treaties sworn
to the Punic, they mark out and cleanse the race of its crime.
The unhappy counsel of those who meant to leave their native land
is punished, and the wicked guilt of Metellus.
Such were the hearts of the men. But indeed not even the women
cease to match the men in mind and demand a share of praise.
Every matron, bearing before herself the ancient glory
of her head and hands and the necklaces stripped from her neck,
rushes in rivalry and they serve the war.
They are not grieved that the men in such a time yielded them
so great a lot of praise, and they rejoice to have given place
to a deed that will go down through the ages. Then the lofty throng
of the senate follows. Into the common store, with great rivalry,
private wealth is heaped. To strip their households
and to have set aside nothing in secret for the uses of a better life
pleases them. The crowd too gathers, without a name.
Thus using all her body and all her limbs, Rome,
though bloodless, again raised her face to the heavens.

The men carrying responses from Parnassian Cirrha
add a sweet hope to the wretched. For they brought glad word
that they had heard in the sanctuaries, when the cavern thundered
with a sacred voice, and the priestess, now entered by Phoebus, bellowed:
'Loose from your hearts, race of Venus, your heavier fears:
adversity, and whatever of hardship remained beneath war,
is drained for you. The lighter of your toils remain,
and terror without ruin. Only bear to the gods your vows
and prayers, and pour warm blood upon the altars,
and do not give your backs to your woes. The war god will be present,
and the Delian seer himself will turn aside the nearer perils,
known ever to have lessened the Trojans' toils.
But indeed, but indeed before all let a hundred altars smoke,
festal, for Jove: let a hundred victims fall to the knives.
He, violent, will drive the grim cloud of war and its savage
storms into Libya: you yourselves will behold
him shaking the aegis into the battles, the world thrown into tumult.'
And after this, proclaimed in the caverns of Parnassus,
was brought, and the god's word reached the ears of the crowd,
in rivalry they climb to the Capitoline citadels,
and prostrate themselves to Jove and honour his shrine with blood;
then they sing the paean and pray for faithful responses.

Meanwhile the elder Torquatus, in his accustomed arms,
was shaking the Sardinian lands with his country's soldiery.
For Hampsagoras, boasting a name from Trojan origin,
had called the Tyrians to renewed war.
The man had a fair son, not worthy of such a parent,
Hostus, on whose gleaming youth relying,
he himself, harsh to peace, rekindled his green years, weak though they were,
in zeal for the ways of barbarous war.
And he, when he sees Torquatus bearing his standards in haste,
hurried, and right hands eager for battle approaching,
flies out by the deceit of a place he knew, through the hidden trackless
glens, and, seizing the foreseen shortcuts of flight,
is covered by the thicketed valley and the leafy shadows.

An island, walled round by the wave-sounding deep,
is steepened by the waters and, pressed by the eddy, contains
its huge lands under the likeness of a bare foot:
hence it was first called Ichnusa by the Greek settlers.
Soon Sardus of Libya, trusting in his noble blood
from Hercules, changed the names of the land after himself.
The Teucrians too flowed in and set their compelled seats there,
scattered over the sea after Pergama was uprooted.
Nor was it a small glory, Iolaus, that you gave to those lands,
your column of Thespiads brought with your father's fleet.
The tale is that, when Actaeon, his limbs mangled,
paid a lamentable penalty for Diana seen in the spring,
the parent, astonished at the strangeness of the woe,
fled, Aristaeus, across the straits and went to the Sardinian retreats.
They say his mother Cyrene showed him the new shores.
The land is clean of serpents and widowed of poisons,
but grim in its climate and tainted by much marsh.
Where it sees Italy, parched on its rocky ridge,
it troubles the straits with its crags far and wide, and within
cooks the pallid fields too much, the south winds smoking under the Crab.
The rest is nourished by the favour of bounteous Ceres.

The land being of this nature, Hostus, eluding Torquatus
often through the wooded pathless wastes, awaited the Sidonian
weapons of war and his Iberian comrades of the toil.
And they, when by the ships' arrival they swelled their courage,
no delay: he bursts from his hiding-places, and far and wide
the opposing columns bristle, and they seem at length to come together
and join step. They seize the open intervals of the spreading
plain with their hurled spears from afar,
until they reach the tried swords, the most faithful weapons.
Then a dire plague: they cut down and fall,
and by turns leave their souls on the savage blade.

I could not indeed hope to unfold worthily the countless
slaughters and so many grim deeds, in proportion to so great
a name of the matter, nor match in words the heat of the warriors.
But you, Calliope, grant to my labour
that the too little-known deeds of a great man be handed on
to long ages, and let us consecrate the honour due to the bard.

Ennius, of the ancient line of King Messapus,
was mingling in the foremost ranks, and adorned with the proud
glory of the Latin vine-staff his right hand. The rugged land
of the Calabrians sent him: ancient Rudiae bore him,
Rudiae now a name memorable only for its nursling.
He in the first fight (as the Thracian bard once,
when Cyzicus shook the Argo, hostile to war,
hurled Rhodopean darts, his quill laid by)
had made himself worthy of beholding by no small slaughter
of men, and the ardour of his hand swelled with killings.
Hostus flies up, hoping it would be eternal glory
if he should beat down so great a stain, and balances his spear with all his strength.
Apollo, sitting in a cloud, laughed at the attempts of his vain
enterprise and sent the weapon off afar into the winds,
and over this: 'Too much, youth, and of too proud
a hope have you drunk. This man is sacred, and a great care
of the Aonian sisters, and a bard worthy of Apollo.
He first shall sing the Italian wars in illustrious verse
and shall raise the leaders to heaven; he shall teach Helicon
to resound in Latin measures, nor shall he yield in honour
or fame to the Ascraean elder.' So Phoebus, and through Hostus's
two temples the avenging arrow runs.
By the youth's fall the stricken columns are turned across the fields,
and the scattered bands alike give their backs.
Then the father, turbid with wrath at hearing of his son's death,
groaning a barbarous and monstrous groan, pierces
his panting breast and urges his steps to his son's shades.

But the leader of Libya, broken by Marcellus and bruised
by the keen fight, had condemned the plains and arms:
he had turned to the wretched Acerrae of unequal war.
Thence, when he had given over the city to flames and swords,
with wrath no lighter nor more sparing he flung himself
upon Nuceria and levelled its walls with the ground.
Afterward Casilinum, having struggled much against him
with the unfair arms of its defenders, with difficulty by craft
he unbarred its thresholds and weighed the besieged ones' lives with gold.
And now, pouring his columns into the Daunian fields,
he bent his fury wherever plunder or wrath had called.
Petelia smoked, burned, its roofs overthrown,
unhappy for its faith and second to wretched Saguntum,
yet once proud to have guarded the Herculean quiver.

Tarentum too had turned its mind to Tyrian undertakings,
and the Punic had entered the gates. But indeed in the gleaming citadel,
trusting the place, an Ausonian band sat thronged.
Here, doing wondrous things, the fleet that lay hidden in the harbour
stood (for from the narrow jaws the sea
bursts out among the rocks and into a broad recess
pours the deep, sundered from the main)—
the ships, then, shut in, which had no way to swim out
with the citadel set above, by craft he carried beyond the barriers of the sea
and bore the keels, transported, through the lands behind.
Slippery runners were set beneath on oaken wagons,
and the wheel, gliding on the hide of a newly slain bullock,
drew the sea-going ship through the grass.
And now, driven over the hills and thickets to the shore,
the fleet swam upon the deep, coming without a rower.

Meanwhile a messenger fills him, terrifying the straits
with the heat of his cares, the keels borne in no usual way,
while far off he longs to storm the Oebalian grandsons
and first to furrow the lands with naval beaks,
telling him the walls of Capua are besieged: the very bars
of the gates wrenched off, and all the war rushing on the wretched.
Fierce, he leaves his undertakings, and, shame adding wings
and wrath alike, with monstrous speed through the nearest lands
he flies off and, threatening, is borne to the eager combats.
Just as if a tigress, roused by the loss of her cub,
darts forth, the Caucasus, astonished, is ranged over in a few hours
and the Ganges crossed at a winged bound,
until with her lightning course she gathers the tracks
of her young and spends her rage on the foe she has seized.

To meet him Centenius, his column scattered, in haste
is poured out, ill in daring and ready for perils,
but a small glory for Hannibal. For, having discharged the honour
of the vine-staff, he had suddenly roused the Latin peasants
and thrown the half-armed band to be laid low by the foe.
Twice seven thousand sent to death (nor did the column halt),
twice seven, which Fulvius, not more skilful with the sword
but notable for his birth, led in lawful arms:
but equally over the bodies of the fallen, poured down,
the way was seized, and the victor, suffering no delay, went on.
A funeral alone held back the fame and the name of that man,
willing as he was to a merciful mind, with a glad burial.
For by treachery, unspeakable, and slain by his host,
while he sought a parley and the perfidious promises of the Lucanian
race, Gracchus, surrounded by blind craft,
had fallen, and the Libyan snatched the praise of burying him.

But now, when the Punic was known to be hastening to the walls,
no affair stood in its place: now both consuls
were present, headlong, all the force from Nola, and from Arpi
Fabius, fresher in years, was bearing his swift arms.
Hence Nero, and hence flying Silanus night and day
drove on, urging the cohorts to the hastened wars.
From every side they gather, and it pleases the leaders alike
to set all of them against the one youth. He himself, lofty,
sits on Tifata, where a hill stands nearer the walls
and from its mounds looks down on the city below.
But when he sees, with so many arms surrounding him,
the allied gates walled up, and that he is denied
both to enter and to burst out of Capua,
anxious at the outcome, now he meditates to break by iron
the throng of those who block him, now he takes pathless
counsels for his enterprise and seeks by craft to draw so many thousands
from the narrowed gates and to unbind the ringed walls.
So therefore with himself, and thus in his heart he wearies his cares:
'Where, sick mind, do you call me? Shall I again take up perils,
unfavoured by the lie of the place, and, with Capua watching,
give my back? Or, sitting on the summit of the neighbouring mountain,
shall I suffer the allied houses to be cut down before my eyes?
Not so did Fabius and the master of the Fabii find me
confounded, when I escaped, victor, the hills shut up
with Hesperian soldiery, and goaded the bullocks scattered through the fields
to toss the fires on their kindled horns.
Not all my wiles have yet departed. If it is snatched from us
to defend Capua, it shall be granted to surround Rome.'

After these things pleased him, and the resolve held his mind,
without waiting until Titan should bring forth his breathing horses
with the light from the deep, he drives his men into the column
with voice and hand and unfolds his monstrous undertakings:
'Go on, come, conquer every toil, soldier, by your valour,
and as far as human strides can stretch themselves,
hasten, lofty. You seek Rome. The Alps paved this road,
Cannae paved it for you. Come, strike against the walls
of Troy your shield-boss, and repay the ruins of Capua:
how worth it will have been to fall, that you may see the Palatine
and the Thunderer departing from his Tarpeian seat.'
Spurred on, they mass their steps. Rome clings to their ears,
Rome to their eyes, and they believe, by the leader's skilful acts,
this undertaking fitter than if he had led them from the very
plain fatal to the Aeneadae. They cross the Volturnus's swift
fords in their boat and the last leave behind,
to delay the Italians, the keels they have spoiled with fire.
Then with nimble maniples they gather the Sidicine fields
and Thracian Cales, your homes, Orithyia, named from your son.
Hence the Allifan land, not unloved by Bacchus,
and the country dwelt in by the Casinian nymphs,
is laid waste. Soon too the neighbouring Aquinas
and Fregellae, which covered the smoking Giant,
are seized by the flying column. Then, roused, he bears
his step over the lofty ridges, where warlike Frusino
clings to hard crags, and grain-bearing Anagnia of Ceres
rises, hung upon its swelling ridge with fruitful clods.
And now indeed he has entered the plains and the fields of Labici,
leaving behind the walls of Telegonus, battered by the ram,
a delay unworthy amid such great things. Nor does pleasant
Algidum hold him back, nor near it the temple of Gabine Juno.
Headlong he is borne to the banks with a monstrous whirlwind,
where, cold, Anio creeps gently with its sulphurous waves,
gliding without a murmur to its father Thybris.

Here, when the fierce one had set his standards and his measured camp
and his cavalry made the banks tremble, terrified
Ilia first hid herself, the fords stirred, in the sacred cave
of her husband, and all the nymphs fled the eddy.
But the Latin mothers, as if no walls remained,
astonished, wander everywhere with frenzied steps.
Before their eyes stand the mangled shades of the trembling dead,
those who at the grievous Trebia and those who at the Ticinus's streams
met their deaths: Paulus and Gracchus, bloody,
and Flaminius together, wander before the faces of the wretched.
The crowd blocked the ways. Lofty and harsh with wrath
the senate stands and with grim face tames the vast fear.
At times, however, beneath the helmet there burst forth
silent tears poured out: what does Fortune threaten,
or what do the gods prepare? The youth, dispersed through the high
towers, stands, and turns over this in their hearts:
that it has come to this, that Rome now thinks it enough to defend her walls.
When the Punic had scarcely indulged his men, driven the whole night
in marching, in sleep, himself wakeful and easy
to no rest, and believing that the time which sleep takes away
is withdrawn from life, he clothes himself in gleaming arms
and bids the squadrons of the Numidians burst forth.
Then, light on his reins, he is borne with hoof-beating sound
around the walls of stricken Rome as they tremble.
Now he surveys the approaches, now with his spear, hostile,
he strikes the closed gates and enjoys the dread of the fearful.
Now, lingering, standing on the lofty hills, he enters
the city with his eyes and learns the places and the causes of the places.
And he would have gathered all with his sight and penetrated
into every part by gazing, had not Fulvius been at hand
with great force, the siege of Capua not wholly left behind.
Then at last the leader bent his exulting squadrons toward the camp,
sated in his breast with Rome beheld.
And when night was driven from the sky and Neptune
reddens with his first lamp, and Dawn recalls men to their labours,
he pours out his columns, leaping over the broken rampart,
and, as loud as he can cry: 'By your many glories,
O comrades, and your right hands sacred in blood,
go equal to yourselves and dare as much under arms
as Rome fears. Cut down this remaining mass:
nothing will be left in all the world for you to conquer.
Nor let the origin of a war-born people slow you:
you will take a city entered by thousands of the Senones
and used to being taken. Perhaps on their lofty curule chairs
even now, by the example of their forefathers, the old men
await a noble death in their custom and make themselves ready for death.'
With such words the Punic here; but on the other side the Oenotrian
youth need no voices of their leader or precepts.
Their mothers stir them enough, and their children, and the dear
faces of their parents, weeping, stretching out their upturned palms.
They show their little ones and with wailing strike the moved
hearts of the men, and fix kisses on their armed right hands.
They wish to go and to set their breasts, packed close, before the walls,
and they look back at their own and swallow back their tears.
But when, the hinge struck, the gates were opened
and at once the army burst out with its arms set in motion,
a clangour is poured, mingled with groaning and prayers,
over the high walls to the sky, and the matrons, scattered,
with loosened hair shriek aloud and bare their breasts.
Fulvius, flying before the column: 'Who would not know,'
he said, 'that the Punic came not of his own will to our homes?
He flees from the gates of Capua.' As he tried to add more,
a grim crash with a vast murmur of the sky troubled him,
and storms from a sudden cloud.
Jupiter, returning from the land of the Ethiopians,
when he saw the threatening Punic approach the Romulean rampart,
had quickly roused the gods and bidden them defend
the Dardan houses and run apart to the seven citadels.
He himself, sublime on the Tarpeian summit, stirs up all things,
both the winds and the clouds and the wraths of the hail
and the thunderbolts and the thunder and the black storms.
The shaken poles trembled, and the sky is closed
with darkness, and night buries the lands in a blind cloak.
The tempest presses on their eyes, and from the near foe
Rome lies hidden. The flames hurled into the squadrons through the clouds
keep their hissing, and the fire whistles among their limbs.
Here the south wind, here the north, here the African with dusky wings
move wars, with all the force by which the spirits and breasts
of angry Jove can sate themselves. A column of waters flows,
confused with a pitch-black whirlwind and a blackening storm,
and wraps all the plains around with foaming waves.
Lofty from the topmost peak of the mountain
the ruler of the gods balanced the thunderbolts raised in his right hand
and, resolved not to yield to the leader's shield,
struck it. The point at the spear's top melted,
and flowed like a sword caught in the furnace.
But indeed the Sidonian leader, his arms scorched,
stayed his comrades and taught that the blind fire from the clouds
and the murmurs were mixed in vain by the winds.
At last, after the disasters of his comrades and the ruin of the sky,
no foe seen in the storm-clouds, no sword, he bids
the standards be carried back to the camp and rekindles his mournful wraths:
'To the winds, no doubt, and the storms of winter, Rome,
you will owe one day. But the coming light shall never
snatch you from us, though Jupiter himself come down
to the lands.' As, gnashing, he says such things,
behold, a bright radiance flashes from the cleared sky,
and the purged air shines, the clouds dispersed.
The Aeneadae felt the god, and, their weapons laid by,
stretch their submissive right hands to the high Capitol
and ring the mountain's sanctuary with festal laurel.
Then their faces, but now dripping with no small sweat,
they turn now glad to Jove: 'Grant, highest of the gods,
grant, father, that the Libyan fall by a sacred weapon
amid the battles. By no other hand can he be brought down.'
So indeed praying they kept silence, after
Hesperus had taken away the lands with blackening shadows.
When Titan, raising his ruddy lamp, overwhelmed him
and the use of life returned to mortals,
the Punic is present, nor does the Oenotrian youth keep itself
in camp. Not yet were the swords drawn, and only so much ground
lay between for the war as hurled spears
might suffice to cross, when the brightness of the sky
